description: Among the hundreds of blades welded together to form the Iron Throne, one of them has a much older claim to fame. Look carefully and you can spot Glamdring, the sword used by Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings, hidden among the swords of vanquished kings and lords.

title: A Severed Head Was Modelled on George Bush
description: Among the grim row of severed heads on spikes at the end of season one, one of the prop heads was made in the likeness of George W. Bush. Showrunners David Benioff and D.B. Weiss have confirmed it was intentional, tucked in among the beheading scenes for anyone paying close enough attention.

title: Jon Snow's Wall Buddies Share Names With Frodo's Friends
entertainment: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
description: It's a subtle one, but a few of Jon Snow's companions at the Night's Watch share names with Frodo's closest friends from The Lord of the Rings. It's the kind of overlap that feels like a deliberate nod between two of fantasy's biggest sagas rather than a coincidence.

title: The Direwolves Were Played by Northern Inuit Dogs
description: There obviously weren't real wolves running around the Winterfell set, so the direwolves were played by Northern Inuit Dogs, a breed specifically developed to look wolf-like while still being trainable and safe around child actors. Two of the original season one pups, Odin and Thor, went on to become minor celebrities in their own right, complete with their own social media accounts.

title: The Direwolf Litter Was Insured for a Million Pounds Each
description: Odin and Thor, the two Northern Inuit dogs who played the direwolf pups Summer and Grey Wind, weren't treated like ordinary animal actors. Their owner had them insured for a million pounds apiece, and over the years following the show they went on to meet roughly 400,000 fans through appearances and tours.

title: Tyrion's Trial Speech Almost Left Out Jaime
description: Tyrion's furious speech from his jail cell in season four is one of the show's most memorable moments, but Nikolaj Coster-Waldau has said it wasn't originally written to be delivered to Jaime. He pushed for the idea that Tyrion should be speaking directly to his brother, and the writers agreed to rework it that way.

title: It All Started on a Train
description: The whole show basically got greenlit because of a train ride. Moffat and Gatiss were chatting about how much they both loved Holmes on the way to the Doctor Who offices in Cardiff, and Moffat went home and told his wife Sue Vertue about it. She's the one who pushed them to actually pitch it to the BBC.

title: Cumberbatch's Mum Wasn't Convinced
description: Even though the producers only ever wanted Benedict Cumberbatch for the role, his own mother, actress Wanda Ventham, didn't think he was right for it. Her exact complaint was that he 'hadn't got the right nose' for Sherlock Holmes.

title: Watson Almost Regenerated Into a Time Lord First
description: Before Martin Freeman locked down the role of John Watson, Matt Smith actually auditioned for it. He didn't get it, but the producers liked him enough to remember him later when they were casting the Eleventh Doctor on Doctor Who.

title: A Stolen Wallet Nearly Cost Freeman the Role
description: Martin Freeman turned up to his first Watson audition in a foul mood after having his wallet stolen, and it apparently came across as him being uninterested in the part. Thankfully he was in much better spirits for the second audition and it worked out fine.

title: Sherlock Was Nearly Six One-Hour Episodes
description: The original plan for Series One was six standard hour-long episodes. After the pilot was shot in that format, the BBC decided to turn it into more of a TV event and asked for three feature-length 90-minute films instead. Moffat's actually credited that change as one of the reasons the show survived as long as it did, since fitting six episodes around Cumberbatch and Freeman's schedules would've been brutal.

title: The Coat Became a Birthday Present
description: Sherlock's famous coat is a Belstaff, and costume designers tried more than once to give him a lighter summer version, but nothing ever quite matched the original. The coat used in the pilot ended up being bought by Mark Gatiss, who later gave it to Cumberbatch as a birthday present.

title: Molly Hooper Broke the Show's Own Rule
description: Molly was only ever supposed to be a one-scene character stuck in the mortuary of A Study in Pink. Moffat and Gatiss had a personal rule that only characters lifted from the original Conan Doyle stories would get major roles, but Louise Brealey's performance was good enough that they threw that rule out and built her into a recurring part of the cast.

title: Mycroft Nearly Got a Gadget Umbrella
description: Mark Gatiss, who plays Mycroft, apparently kept lobbying Moffat to let Mycroft's umbrella conceal some kind of spy gadget or trick. Moffat shot the idea down every single time.

title: Cumberbatch's Sherlock Training Regime
description: While filming, Cumberbatch cuts out drinking and smoking entirely and gets into swimming and Bikram yoga sessions in a sauna. It's a nice bit of accidental accuracy too, since sauna-going was actually something Holmes enjoyed in Conan Doyle's original stories.

title: The Deleted Sibling Backstory
description: There was originally a scene in The Great Game laying out exactly why Mycroft and Sherlock don't get along, tied to some childhood incident Mycroft blamed on his brother. It got cut in the end, with Moffat and Gatiss deciding the rivalry worked better left a mystery.

title: Moriarty Was Almost Just 'Jim From IT'
description: Andrew Scott's Moriarty was originally only meant to pop up briefly as Molly's boyfriend 'Jim from IT' in The Great Game. The writers were so impressed by him that they hurried to write in the swimming pool confrontation at the end of the episode, and that tense exchange between him and Sherlock was actually lifted straight from Scott's original audition script.

title: Over 100 Complaints About Irene Adler
description: A Scandal in Belgravia caused a bit of a stir when it aired. Lara Pulver's version of Irene Adler as a confident dominatrix who uses her nudity to unsettle Sherlock led to the BBC getting more than 100 complaints from viewers.

title: Moffat Clapped Back on the Feminist Criticism
description: Some fans and critics argued the show's Irene Adler was a step down from Conan Doyle's original, who beats Holmes by simply outsmarting him rather than falling for him. Moffat pushed back on that reading in an interview with The Guardian, pointing out that in the original story Adler's 'victory' was just running off and getting married, which he didn't think counted as much of a feminist win either.

title: Real Violins, Real Money
description: Every violin Sherlock plays on screen across the three series is a genuine instrument on loan from Cardiff Violins, not a prop. The one used in Series Three was reportedly worth around £1200, and the company was apparently pretty touched when the BBC sent it back with a nice letter.

title: The Real Baker Street Was Too Sherlock-y to Film On
description: You'd think the show would film outside the actual 221B Baker Street, but by the time production started there was so much Sherlock Holmes signage and tourist clutter around the real street that it wasn't usable. The crew ended up shooting exteriors about a mile east, on North Gower Street instead.

title: Speedy's Started Out as Mrs Hudson's Snax & Sandwiches
description: The real café next to the North Gower Street flat, which fans know as Speedy's, was actually branded 'Mrs Hudson's Snax & Sandwiches' for the pilot episode before that name got scrapped for the actual series.

title: Sherlock's Parents Are Played by Cumberbatch's Actual Parents
description: Keep an eye out in the opening episode of Series Three, the tea scene at Sherlock's flat with his mum and dad. Those are Cumberbatch's real-life parents, Wanda Ventham and Timothy Carlton, playing Mr and Mrs Holmes.

title: A Finale That Broke UK Twitter
description: One of the show's series finales generated a reported 377,182 tweets, which at the time was the highest tweet count ever recorded for a single episode of a UK drama. Only a Doctor Who anniversary special beat it, and that one's technically classed as a special rather than a normal episode.

title: A Ghost Station Got Used for Filming
description: London's underground has a handful of disused 'ghost stations' that no longer see any trains, and the production used one of them, the closed Aldwych station, while filming The Empty Hearse.

title: The Lucky Cat Emporium Was Never Actually in London
description: Sherlock and Watson are shown strolling down the real Gerrard Street in London's Chinatown in The Blind Banker, but the Lucky Cat Emporium itself, exterior and interior both, was actually shot over in Newport, Wales.

title: Mycroft's Club Is Really an Academy Building
description: The Diogenes Club, the strictly silent gentleman's club where Sherlock goes to see Mycroft, is played on screen by Carlton House Terrace, which in real life is home to the British Academy.

title: Baskerville Is a Real Gas Storage Facility
description: The top-secret military research base in The Hounds of Baskerville is actually the Dynevor Arms Liquefied Natural Gas Storage Facility near Merthyr Tydfil in Wales, and just like the fictional base it's playing, the public still can't get anywhere near it.

title: Eurus's Cell Was Designed So She'd Never Have to Leave It
description: Production designer Arwel Wyn Jones tucked some genuinely eerie details into Eurus's glass cell in Sherrinford. Look closely at the floor and walls and there are scratch marks showing where a toilet, shower, table and bed could all slide out of hidden compartments, meaning she could be left completely alone with nothing visible at all if needed. There's also a round ceiling grate that's a deliberate visual echo of the well she trapped John and 'Redbeard' in as a child.

title: The Show Only Made 10 Episodes in Nearly a Decade
description: Despite the huge fanbase, Sherlock only produced 10 episodes total across almost eight years, a fraction of what a normal weekly network show would churn out in that time. Moffat's argued that's actually part of what let the show keep coming back, since it never has to shoot on a fixed continuous schedule.

title: The Show Was Almost Called Montauk
description: Before Hawkins existed, the Duffer Brothers were shopping around a series called Montauk, set in the real Long Island town and loosely inspired by the actual government conspiracy theories tied to it. Networks passed, they moved the setting to a made-up Midwest town for a broader feel, and renamed it Stranger Things (some say as a nod to Stephen King's Needful Things). There's actually a sly Montauk easter egg tucked into the series finale if you know where to look.

title: Two Separate Lawsuits Claimed the Show Was Stolen
description: The show's origin story hasn't been drama-free off screen either. One filmmaker claimed the Duffers lifted his unmade script Totem, about a young girl with powers, while another accused them of ripping off his short film about the Montauk Project. Both cases were eventually dropped, with one plaintiff even admitting his work had nothing to do with how the series actually came together.

title: The Duffers Regret Killing Off Chrissy
description: Chrissy's brutal death in Season 4 landed as a gut punch for fans who'd just started shipping her with Eddie Munson. Turns out the brothers felt it too. They admitted they filmed the sweet forest scene between the two characters after her fate was already locked in, and only realised how much chemistry Joseph Quinn and Grace Van Dien had once it was too late to change anything.

title: A Bridgerton Star Almost Played Robin
description: Before Maya Hawke made Robin Buckley iconic, Bridgerton's Nicola Coughlan actually auditioned for the part and came close to landing it. She's since said publicly that Hawke absolutely nailed it in a way she doesn't think she could have, which is a pretty gracious thing to admit about a role you nearly got.

title: They Nearly Jumped Decades Each Season
description: There was a point where the Duffers seriously floated the idea of moving each new season forward a decade, starting in the 80s and eventually landing in the present day by Season 5. It would have been a wild ride through changing fashion and pop culture, but they ultimately scrapped it because they realised the heart of the show was really the kids and their journey together, not the era they were stuck in.

title: The Upside Down Used to Be Called 'The Nether'
description: Millie Bobby Brown let this one slip on the Beyond Stranger Things aftershow: in the earliest Season 1 scripts, the parallel dimension wasn't the Upside Down at all, it was 'The Nether'. Way more gothic sounding, sure, but nowhere near as catchy or as easy for a bunch of kids on bikes to yell across a hallway.

title: Sadie Sink Had to Fight for the Role of Max
description: Producers were initially ready to pass on Sadie Sink for Max because, at 14, she was a bit older than the rest of the Hawkins crew and they worried she wouldn't slot into the group dynamic. She refused to take the hint, pushed for more audition material, and once she got a chemistry read with Gaten Matarazzo and Caleb McLaughlin, the part was hers on the spot.

title: Steve Harrington Was Written to Be Much Worse
description: The Steve Harrington fans adore today started life on the page as, in Ross Duffer's own words, 'the biggest douchebag on the planet'. Early drafts had him behaving far more aggressively toward Nancy and heading for an early death in Season 1. Joe Keery's natural charisma is basically the reason the character survived and turned into one of the show's most beloved arcs.

title: Millie Bobby Brown Needed Convincing to Shave Her Head
description: At 11 years old, Millie Bobby Brown was understandably nervous about shaving her head to become Eleven. The Duffers ended up showing her a photo of Charlize Theron as Furiosa in Mad Max: Fury Road, reframing the look as something powerful rather than scary, and it worked. She's said she let out a proper roar the moment she saw the finished buzzcut in the mirror.

title: Millie Bobby Brown's Dad Left the Room Crying During Her Headshave
description: Her mum actually filmed the head-shaving moment, but if you watch the footage that later ended up online, you'll notice her dad isn't in it. According to the Duffer Brothers, that's because watching his daughter go through with it was too much for him and he had to step out of the room before it was finished.

title: Netflix's Predecessors Rejected the Pitch Around 20 Times
description: Long before it became one of the biggest shows on the planet, Stranger Things was turned down by roughly 15 to 20 different networks and studios. Execs weren't sure what to do with a story mixing kids, adults, sci-fi and horror all at once, and some even suggested reworking it into either a straight-up kids show or an adult mystery centred on Hopper. The Duffers held their ground and kept pitching the version they actually wanted to make.

title: Eleven and Steve Were Both Originally Supposed to Die in Season 1
description: Two of the show's most enduring characters nearly never made it past their debut season. Eleven was written to sacrifice herself to save Hawkins, while Steve was meant to stay a flat, unlikeable jerk who wasn't going to last long anyway. It was really the actors themselves, Millie Bobby Brown's intensity and Joe Keery's easy charm, that convinced the Duffers to let both characters live and grow.

title: Kate Bush's 'Running Up That Hill' Hit Number One Decades Later
description: When Max Mayfield uses this 1985 track as her lifeline against Vecna in Season 4, nobody expected it to send a nearly 40-year-old song rocketing back up the charts. Kate Bush herself, notoriously private and rarely public about anything, posted a heartfelt statement thanking the show's young fans for giving the track, in her words, 'a whole new lease of life'.

title: The Duffers Only Made Stranger Things Because They Were Rejected From It
description: While the 2017 remake of Stephen King's It was in early development, Matt and Ross Duffer actually pitched themselves as directors for it and got turned down. Rather than sulk, they redirected all that Stephen King energy into their own passion project instead, which became Stranger Things. There's a nice bit of irony in the fact that Finn Wolfhard, who plays Mike Wheeler, ended up starring in the actual It movies anyway.

title: The Duffers Pranked Noah Schnapp's Mum With a Fake Corpse
description: For the infamous 'body in the quarry' reveal, the props team built an eerily accurate fake corpse of young Will Byers. The Duffer Brothers have admitted they took it a step too far when they surprised Noah Schnapp's own mother with it on set, genuinely startling her before she came round and started taking selfies with the thing.

title: Dacre Montgomery Deliberately Slimmed Down to Play Billy
description: Dacre Montgomery had built a noticeably muscular physique for Power Rangers, but when he landed the role of Billy Hargrove he made a point of shedding that gym-honed look. He wanted Billy to feel like a real teenager from the mid-80s rather than a superhero, and leaned into that more ordinary build to make the character's swagger and menace feel grounded.

title: Dustin's Missing Teeth Are Based on a Real Condition Gaten Matarazzo Has
description: Dustin's claim that he has 'no collarbones' actually points to a genuine condition called cleidocranial dysplasia, which Gaten Matarazzo was born with. The Duffers wrote it directly into the show as an explanation for why the character was missing teeth in the earlier seasons, turning something very personal to the actor into part of Dustin's identity.

title: A Glitter Mishap Once Shut Down Filming
description: During Season 1, Millie Bobby Brown showed up on set inexplicably covered head to toe in glitter, forcing the crew to pause production for nearly 45 minutes while everyone worked to get her cleaned up. The Duffers have said it was one of those moments that reminded them she was still just an 11-year-old kid, despite carrying a show alongside a cast of adults.

title: On-Screen Smoking Sparked a Real Netflix Policy Change
description: Season 3's frequent shots of Joyce and Hopper lighting up cigarettes landed the show on a list of the worst offenders for on-screen tobacco use, according to a Truth Initiative survey. Netflix responded publicly, promising that future projects rated TV-14 or below would go smoke and vape free unless historical accuracy genuinely called for it.

title: Starcourt Mall Was a Real Abandoned 80s Shopping Centre
description: The gloriously nostalgic Starcourt Mall in Season 3 wasn't built from scratch. The crew filmed inside Atlanta's real Gwinnett Place Mall, which actually opened in 1984, just a year before the season is set. The production designer described the location as still holding onto 'echoes' of its original 80s showpiece glory, even with half its stores long abandoned.

title: Robin's Actress Is Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman's Daughter
description: Maya Hawke, who plays the sharp-tongued Robin Buckley from Season 3 onward, is the real-life daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, two actors who defined a lot of 80s and 90s cinema themselves. It's a fun bit of casting trivia that only clicks once you notice the resemblance.

title: Hopper's Cabin Is a Real Escape Room You Can Visit
description: The rustic cabin where Hopper gets attacked in Season 3 cost the production a grand total of one dollar to use, because it belongs to an Atlanta escape room company called Escape Woods. They later turned the actual cabin into one of their own attractions, letting fans try to outsmart their own version of the Mind Flayer on site.

title: Hawkins Lab Was Filmed in a Real Former Psychiatric Hospital
description: The unsettling corridors of Hawkins Lab have been shot inside a genuine decommissioned psychiatric hospital owned by Emory University in Atlanta. The building was actually scheduled for demolition back in 2023, but the writers' and actors' strikes that year delayed filming, which ended up pushing back the building's destruction too.

title: The VFX Team Built a Full-Size Physical Dead Demogorgon
description: For one key Season 5 scene, the visual effects crew didn't just rely on computers. They 3D-printed a full-size Demogorgon corpse, cast it in silicone and rigged it with an articulated frame so it would flop convincingly. The finished thing weighed close to 200 pounds and needed a stretcher and four crew members just to carry it around set.

title: Jamie Campbell Bower Spent 70 Hours Total Becoming Vecna
description: Turning into Vecna wasn't a quick job. Jamie Campbell Bower estimates he clocked around 70 hours across the season sitting in the prosthetics chair, wearing custom contact lenses and dentures so he could still act through all the latex. Season 5 actually required less coverage than before since only his head, shoulders and one arm needed prosthetics, with the rest handled through a tracked bodysuit and digital effects.

title: The Upside Down's Vines Were Built From 27 Miles of Pool Noodles
description: Building out the tangled, organic look of the Upside Down for Season 5 took a genuinely absurd amount of materials, roughly 27.3 miles of pool noodles and 81 miles of rope, all turned into around 52 miles of finished tendrils. One crew member reportedly hand-rubbed 70 percent of the noodles themselves just to keep the texture and colour consistent throughout.

title: A Real 80s Candy Bar Was Recreated for Season 5
description: Steve introduces a chocolate bar called Peanut Butter Boppers in the final season, and it's not a made-up prop. It's a genuine 1980s treat, and the props team went as far as consulting the original manufacturer to recreate the packaging accurately. The timing worked out nicely too, since the company ended up rereleasing the actual bar not long after the show came out.

title: Doc and Mharti
description: Long before Adult Swim got involved, Rick and Morty existed as a scrappy little animated short Justin Roiland made back in 2006 called The Real Animated Adventures of Doc and Mharti. It was basically a filthy, unfiltered parody of Doc Brown and Marty McFly, and you can still spot the DNA of the finished show all over it.

title: The Accidental Catchphrase
description: Wubba Lubba Dub Dub wasn't even in the script. The line called for Rick to yell 'Woob woob woob' like Curly from The Three Stooges, but Roiland is dyslexic and just blurted out the wrong words entirely. Everyone in the booth loved it so much it stuck, and the writers later decided it secretly means 'I am in great pain, please help me.'

title: Bryan Cranston Almost Played Jerry
description: While he was still playing Walter White on Breaking Bad, Bryan Cranston actually auditioned for the role of Jerry Smith. He lost out to Chris Parnell, which honestly feels like the universe course-correcting, because it's very hard to imagine Heisenberg's voice coming out of Rick and Morty's most useless dad.

title: Season Three's Writers Room Shake-Up
description: For the first two seasons the writers room was basically all guys running around having Nerf gun fights and Lego competitions between pitches. Season three changed that with the show's first gender-balanced room, and both Harmon and Roiland have said the female writers brought in that year were a huge part of why the Beth and Summer storylines got so much stronger.

title: A Canadian Studio Runs the Multiverse
description: The actual animation isn't done in-house, it's handled by a Canadian studio called Bardel Entertainment, who also work on shows like The Dragon Prince and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. Fittingly weird bonus detail, their CEO happens to genuinely be named Rick.

title: Mr. Poopybutthole Was Retroactively Added
description: Mr. Poopybutthole technically first shows up in Total Rickall, but the production team went back and edited him into the memory scenarios shown in that episode's own opening scenes to sell the joke that he'd secretly always been part of the family. So depending how you look at it, he was either never there before, or he always was.

title: The First Instagram TV Premiere
description: Adult Swim rolled out Rixty Minutes before it actually aired on TV, splitting it into 109 separate 15-second clips posted to Instagram. Nobody had done that before, which technically makes it the very first television episode premiere to happen on Instagram.

title: Doofus Rick's Sad Morty
description: Doofus Rick's Morty is drawn to resemble actor Eric Stoltz, who was actually cast as Marty McFly and had already filmed a chunk of Back to the Future before the studio quietly swapped him out for Michael J. Fox. It's a deep-cut Hollywood reference hiding in plain sight in one of the show's saddest side characters.

title: Evil Morty's Theme Song
description: That eyepatch-wearing Morty who shows up briefly back in season one turns out to be the mastermind running the entire Citadel of Ricks election storyline in The Ricklantis Mixup. The second the show confirms he's Evil Morty, For the Damaged Coda by Blonde Redhead kicks in, and the band's music has basically become his unofficial theme ever since.

title: The South Park Slow Burn
description: In one episode Rick and Morty get interrupted mid-Minecraft session, and when Morty complains, Rick just shrugs that South Park already did this joke four years earlier. Morty replies that they're fast, and Rick corrects him that actually they're just slow, a cheeky nod to the fact South Park writes and airs episodes within the same week while Rick and Morty doesn't release anything until a whole season is finished.

title: The Sauce That Started a Riot
description: A throwaway dream sequence in The Rickshank Rickdemption, where Rick rants about a 1998 McDonald's promo tie-in dipping sauce, turned into one of the strangest fandom moments in TV history. When McDonald's actually brought Szechuan Sauce back for one day in October 2017, the tiny supply sent to stores caused genuine chaos, with police called out to calm crowds chanting for more.

title: McDonald's Had to Apologize
description: The Szechuan Sauce fiasco got so out of hand that McDonald's put out a public apology admitting their limited batch clearly wasn't enough for the demand, and promised a proper, much wider re-release. That relaunch finally happened in February 2018, and this time it went off without a single reported incident.

title: Justin Roiland Wasn't Happy Either
description: Roiland actually distanced himself from the whole Szechuan Sauce mess in real time, tweeting that the show had nothing to do with how McDonald's handled the promotion and asking fans to be cool to the employees, since none of it was their fault.

title: Method Acting, Rick Sanchez Style
description: To really nail Rick's drunken cadence, Roiland used to drink water and beer during recording sessions specifically so he could burp mid-line on cue. He apparently took that dedication even further once, recording a session after several shots of tequila and a few beers, and reportedly thought he still sounded too sober and asked for one more round, which the crew flatly refused.

title: Pickle Rick Premiered a Year Early
description: A rough, unfinished animatic of the Pickle Rick sewer sequence was shown off to fans at San Diego Comic-Con back in 2016, a full year before the finished episode actually aired on Adult Swim. Some fans even spent that year convinced it was some kind of elaborate April Fools joke because it took so long to show up on screen.

title: Pickle Rick Was Basically a Breaking Bad Homage
description: Dan Harmon has said the whole concept behind Pickle Rick was directly inspired by the Breaking Bad episode 4 Days Out, where Walt and Jesse get stranded in the desert and have to survive using nothing but their wits and whatever junk is lying around. Swap the desert for a sewer full of rats and you've basically got Rick's version of the same survival story.

title: The Show's First Emmy
description: Pickle Rick didn't just become a fan favorite, it also won Rick and Morty its first ever Emmy, taking home Outstanding Animated Program at the 2018 Creative Arts Emmys. It beat out some genuinely stiff competition that year, including episodes of The Simpsons, Bob's Burgers, and South Park.

title: Pickle Rick Got His Own Pringles Flavor
description: The love for Pickle Rick got so big that Pringles announced a dedicated Pickle Rick flavored can, timed to launch right around Super Bowl weekend in early February 2020, giving the murderous gherkin a genuinely bizarre second life as a snack food.

title: Sixteen Bite-Sized Claymation Shorts
description: Between October 2016 and July 2017, Adult Swim quietly slipped sixteen tiny stop-motion Claymation shorts into their ad breaks, each one putting Rick and Morty into parodies of famous film scenes rendered entirely in clay.

title: Roiland's Video Game Studio Named After Squanchy
description: In 2016 Justin Roiland launched his own game studio and called it Squanchtendo, a mashup of the show's promiscuous alien Squanchy and Nintendo. He later renamed it Squanch Games at the end of 2017, and it went on to make the VR title Rick and Morty: Virtual Rick-ality and the sci-fi comedy game High on Life.

title: The End of Justin Roiland's Rick and Morty Era
description: After domestic violence and misconduct allegations became public in January 2023, Adult Swim publicly cut ties with Justin Roiland, who had voiced both Rick and Morty since the series began in 2013. Dan Harmon stayed on as sole showrunner, and the show was recast for season seven, which premiered later that year with new actors stepping into the roles.

title: Rick's Backstory Is Deliberately Half-Told
description: Harmon and Roiland have admitted there's a huge, detailed backstory for Rick worked out behind the scenes that fans will probably never see in full. They've said they deliberately only drip-feed small pieces of it through the show, because they think the mystery is funnier and more interesting than a full explanation would be.

title: A Recurring Alien Cameo
description: Keep an eye on the background during any of the show's big interdimensional or portal-hopping episodes, there's a small pink and blue alien creature that the animators have snuck into pretty much every single one of them as a running visual gag for eagle-eyed fans.

title: It Was Almost a Live-Action Film
description: Before it was ever an animated show, Invincible was being developed as a live-action movie back in 2017 through Universal Pictures. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg, both massive fans of the comic, were attached as producers, and their company Point Grey Pictures is still part of the production credits on the show today.

title: 144 Issues, One Ending
description: The Invincible comic wrapped up in 2018 after a 144-issue run that started way back in 2003. Robert Kirkman co-created it with artist Cory Walker, with Ryan Ottley taking over the pencils for most of the series' life. The animated show wasn't even publicly announced until a few months after the final issue hit shelves.

title: Amazon Ordered It Sight Unseen for Eight Episodes
description: Amazon officially greenlit the series on June 19, 2018, committing to a first season of eight episodes right out of the gate rather than a pilot order. That's a pretty rare vote of confidence for an adult animated show nobody outside comic circles had heard of yet.

title: Renewed for Two Seasons Before Season One Even Finished
description: Amazon didn't wait around to see how audiences reacted. Just ahead of the Season 1 finale in April 2021, the platform locked in both Season 2 and Season 3 in one go, with Kirkman saying at the time that the response had exceeded anything he expected.

title: J.K. Simmons Wasn't Supposed to Play Omni-Man
description: When the team first approached J.K. Simmons, they actually had him in mind for Cecil Stedman, the shady government fixer. Simmons read the script and told them he'd rather play Omni-Man instead. Kirkman and the writers agreed on the spot, and Walton Goggins ended up taking the Cecil role instead.

title: Simmons Didn't Clock How Dark Nolan Was At First
description: Because he'd only read the first couple of scripts before signing on, Simmons initially thought Omni-Man was just going to be another warm, wise TV dad. It wasn't until later scripts arrived that he realised exactly what kind of character he'd actually agreed to play.

title: The Original Comic Artist Helped Shape the Animation
description: Cory Walker, who drew the earliest issues of the comic alongside Kirkman, didn't just hand the property over and walk away. He came on board as lead artist and executive producer for the show, working to make sure the animated designs still felt true to his original linework.

title: Season One Was 80% Hand-Drawn
description: The first season was brought to life by Vancouver studio Wind Sun Sky Entertainment under CEO Catherine Winder, using a mix of roughly 80% traditional hand-drawn animation and 20% CG. It's part of why the early episodes have such a distinct, slightly old-school comic feel compared to a lot of modern animation.

title: Skybound Built Its Own In-House Animation Team
description: Wind Sun Sky only handled Season 1. After that, Kirkman's company Skybound set up its own dedicated animation arm to take over key frame work for the rest of the series, which is part of why the visual style noticeably shifted from Season 2 onward.

title: The School Principal Is Named After Family Matters
description: Mark's high school principal is voiced by Reginald VelJohnson and, fittingly, the school itself is called Reginald VelJohnson High. His character is named B.N. Winslow, a direct nod to Carl Winslow, the role that made VelJohnson a household name on Family Matters. He's probably better known to some fans as the cop who helps John McClane in Die Hard, too.

title: Rick and Morty's Creator Has a Blink-and-Miss-It Cameo
description: In episode 6 of Season 1, the drunk jock that D.A. Sinclair kidnaps is voiced by Justin Roiland, the co-creator and voice of Rick Sanchez himself. It's an easy one to miss since the character barely appears, but the voice is unmistakable once you know to listen for it.

title: One Actor Voices Two Villains, and It's a Walking Dead Wink
description: Phil Lamarr, who plays Lucan in the main cast, also lends his voice to a villain called The Walking Dread, a hulking, zombie-faced brute who can absorb energy. The name is a not-so-subtle tip of the hat to Kirkman's other big franchise, and Lamarr voicing both just makes the joke land harder.

title: Megatron Voices a Viltrumite Emperor
description: When Emperor Argall finally shows up and speaks in Season 4, the voice belongs to Frank Welker, best known as the original voice of Megatron in the 1980s Transformers cartoon. Having him face off against Peter Cullen's Thaedus, the show's Optimus Prime, is a deliberate bit of stunt casting that Transformers fans clocked instantly.

title: The Spider-Man Cameo Needed Amazon's Legal Team
description: When Invincible crossed into other comic universes during the Angstrom Levy arc, director Dan Duncan pushed to cast Josh Keaton as the Spider-Man stand-in, since Keaton had voiced Spidey in The Spectacular Spider-Man and later Across the Spider-Verse. Getting the design past Amazon's lawyers took some back and forth, apparently mostly arguments over what colour the costume was allowed to be.

title: The Cast Is Stacked With Walking Dead Veterans
description: It's not just Steven Yeun. Several other actors from The Walking Dead turn up across the show's voice cast, which makes sense given Kirkman created both properties. It's become something of a running theme for eagle-eyed fans to spot who's crossed over from Woodbury or Alexandria into Mark Grayson's world.

title: Danai Gurira Joined a Year After Jeffrey Dean Morgan
description: Season 4 brought in Danai Gurira to voice the villain Universa, arriving almost exactly a year after fellow Walking Dead alum Jeffrey Dean Morgan had his own turn in the series. Kirkman clearly isn't shy about pulling from his old cast list when a role fits.

title: The Composer Also Scored Maze Runner and Daredevil
description: John Paesano handles the score for Invincible, and outside the show he's the guy behind the music for the Maze Runner film trilogy and Marvel's Daredevil series, along with several Spider-Man video games. His work on Invincible earned its own soundtrack release, split across volumes covering the different seasons.

title: There's a Standalone Atom Eve Special
description: Not long after the Season 2 trailer dropped, Amazon quietly released a separate Atom Eve special dedicated to fleshing out Samantha Eve Wilkins' backstory before she became a bigger part of the main storyline. It's an easy one to overlook if you're only tracking numbered episodes.

title: Season 3 Became Prime Video's Biggest Animated Season Ever
description: By the numbers, Season 3 turned out to be the most-watched animated season Prime Video has ever put out, and the biggest returning season across every adult animation title on the platform. Not bad for a show that started out as a mid-budget adaptation of a mid-2000s indie comic.

title: Season 3 Picked Up Back-to-Back Emmy Nominations
description: The show landed consecutive Primetime Emmy nominations in both 2024 and 2025, and Season 3 was also nominated for the Critics' Choice Award for Best Animated Series in 2025, cementing it as one of the more critically respected superhero shows on TV right now, animated or otherwise.

title: Lee Pace Joined the Cast to Play Thragg
description: Season 4 brought in some heavy hitters, with Lee Pace stepping in to voice Thragg, one of the show's most dangerous Viltrumite threats, alongside Matthew Rhys joining the cast in the same run. It's part of a pattern of the show continuing to pull in bigger names as the story escalates.

title: There's a Fighting Game Built on Unreal Engine 5
description: Invincible VS, a fighting game spun off from the show, was developed by Quarter Up and published through Skybound Games, releasing on April 30, 2026 for PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC, and arcades. Several of the animated series' actual voice cast came back to reprise their characters for it, including J.K. Simmons as Omni-Man.

title: Walton Goggins Isn't New to Superhero Movies
description: Before he took on the role of Cecil Stedman, Walton Goggins had already dipped a toe into the genre playing Sonny Burch in Ant-Man and the Wasp. His casting as the calculating head of the Global Defense Agency in Invincible fits a pattern where a lot of the show's cast had prior comic book adaptation experience before joining.

title: Henry Cavill Basically Begged For The Role
description: Cavill wasn't just cast, he campaigned for it. He'd been a huge fan of the books and games long before Netflix got involved, and once he heard a show was in the works he kept pushing his agents to get him a meeting. Showrunner Lauren Schmidt Hissrich actually tested over 200 other actors for Geralt before she gave in and let him read.

title: The Crying Baby Problem
description: In the season one carriage attack scene, the production used a real baby for the shot, and unsurprisingly it would not stop crying on cue. The team ended up leaning on VFX to fake several elements of that sequence, including the sword strikes hitting the carriage walls.

title: Elder Speech Is A Real Constructed Language
description: The magic users of the Continent, like Geralt and Yennefer, don't just mutter fantasy gibberish when they cast spells. Elder Speech is treated as its own proper in-world language throughout the series, separate from the English used for everyday dialogue.

title: The Reavers' Accent Came From The Stunt Team
description: Steve Wall, who plays Boholt, wasn't a fan of the East London-style accent the Reavers use in the games. Instead he based his own take on the character on the Slovakian fight choreographers he was working alongside on set, which is why Boholt sounds nothing like his game counterpart.

title: Yennefer And Jaskier's Actors Are Genuinely Best Mates
description: Anya Chalotra and Joey Batey aren't just playing well against each other on screen. The two have said in multiple interviews that they became close friends during filming and still do joint press together, which probably explains why their scenes have such easy chemistry.

title: The Bathtub Scene Is A Deliberate Game Reference
description: Geralt's infamous nude bathtub moment wasn't just fan service for the sake of it, it's a direct nod to a similarly iconic scene from The Witcher 3. Unlike the game, though, the show actually gives the moment proper narrative context pulled from the source novels rather than just dropping it in.

title: Cavill Wrecked His Eyes Filming In The Canary Islands
description: Geralt's contacts weren't kind to Henry Cavill. He was told never to wear them for more than three hours at a stretch because of the damage they could cause, but he kept them in longer anyway, and while shooting in the Canary Islands, volcanic dust got trapped behind the lenses and scratched his eyes badly enough that he could barely open them.

title: A Whole Monster Fight Got Cut For Money
description: Season three's fourth episode opens with Geralt walking into an inn already covered in Selkie Maw blood and guts. The full fight was originally meant to be shown on screen, and concept art for it exists, but it got axed because the budget couldn't stretch that far.

title: The Showrunner Came From The West Wing And Daredevil
description: Lauren Schmidt Hissrich wasn't a fantasy specialist before taking this on. Her résumé includes writing and producing credits on The West Wing, Parenthood, and Marvel's Daredevil and The Defenders, a pretty different toolkit that she brought over to building the Continent.

title: The Games' Cinematics Director Pitched The Whole Show
description: Tomek Baginski, who directed the cinematic trailers for the video games, is the one who originally pitched The Witcher to Netflix, and he stayed on as an executive producer through the show's production. His own company is behind the series as well.

title: Ropes Made The Striga Fly
description: The Striga's leaping attacks in season one weren't done with pure CGI. Stunt coordinators relied heavily on ropework, essentially rigging the performers to wires and yanking them through the air, to sell the monster's speed and the scene where it crashes through the floor with Geralt.

title: Liam Hemsworth Officially Takes Over As Geralt
description: Starting with season four, Liam Hemsworth stepped into the role of Geralt of Rivia for the final two seasons of the show, alongside Laurence Fishburne joining as the centuries-old vampire barber-surgeon Regis.

title: Seasons Four And Five Were Shot Back To Back
description: Rather than shooting one season, wrapping, and starting fresh later, the production filmed season four and the upcoming fifth and final season together in one continuous stretch, which is how the show plans to close out its story.

title: Old Scenes Got Digitally Reshot With The New Actor's Face
description: To smooth over the recast, the show didn't just move on quietly. Showrunner Lauren Schmidt Hissrich has said they went back and reshot pivotal older moments with Liam Hemsworth in them instead of Henry Cavill, specifically so the change wouldn't feel glossed over.

title: The Season Four Recap Quietly Swaps Geralt's Face
description: Watch the opening recap of season four closely and you'll notice the Butcher of Blaviken flashback, originally Henry Cavill's scene from the very first episode, now plays out with Liam Hemsworth's face instead. It's framed as a story being retold generations later by an unreliable narrator, which is the show's clever in-universe excuse for the switch.

title: Hemsworth Went Quiet Online For A Year Over Backlash
description: The recasting announcement didn't go down well with a lot of fans, and Liam Hemsworth reportedly stepped away from social media for roughly a year to avoid the pile-on before his first season as Geralt even aired.

title: Season One Was Basically Built In Budapest
description: A huge chunk of season one's Continent was actually Hungary. The town of Blaviken and the great hall of Cintra were both built as sets at Mafilm and Origo Studios near Budapest, with the crew also shooting real locations like the Kiscelli Museum for the Aretuza scenes.

title: COVID Forced Kaer Morhen To Move To London
description: Season one traveled across Hungary, Poland, and Spain, but the pandemic made that kind of globe-trotting impossible for season two. So the entire season, including the witchers' stronghold Kaer Morhen, ended up being built and filmed at Arborfield Film Studios, a converted former army barracks outside London.

title: Yennefer's Hometown Was Shot At An Open-Air Folk Museum
description: Vengerberg, the town Yennefer grew up in, was filmed at the Szentendre Skanzen Village Museum in Hungary, a site normally dedicated to preserving traditional Carpathian folk architecture rather than housing fictional sorceresses.

title: The Canary Islands Doubled As Both Desert And Dryad Forest
description: The dune landscapes of Gran Canaria stood in for the sea of sand Geralt has to cross on his travels, while nearby jungle and coastline on the islands were used to bring the Dryads' Brokilon Forest to life. Same set of islands, two very different biomes.

title: An Austrian Castle Plays The Ruined City Of Vizima
description: The abandoned castle of Vizima in Temeria is actually Kreuzenstein Castle near Leobendorf, Austria. Its exteriors gave the production a genuinely ancient, weathered look that would have been far harder to fake on a soundstage.

title: The Show's Biggest Song Was Written Before Filming Even Started
description: "Toss a Coin to Your Witcher" wasn't added in post or written on a whim, composers Sonya Belousova and Giona Ostinelli finished it back in November 2018, well before production began, because Joey Batey needed the finished track to actually perform on camera as Jaskier.

title: The Song Doesn't Exist In The Books At All
description: As catchy as it is, "Toss a Coin to Your Witcher" was created purely for the Netflix adaptation. It has no equivalent in Sapkowski's original novels, it was written specifically to give the show its own musical identity.

title: Joey Batey Recorded It While Sick
description: Batey wasn't in great shape when it came time to record the song properly. He turned up to the studio unwell, got through the session on multiple cups of honey and lemon tea, and still managed to nail several clean takes.

title: Arcane Was Announced at League's 10th Birthday Party
description: Riot first teased Arcane back in October 2019, dropping it as a surprise during League of Legends' 10th anniversary celebrations. CEO Nicolo Laurent said at the time they were already planning for multiple seasons, which is a bold claim to make before a single frame had aired.

title: The Show Was Originally Meant for 2020
description: Arcane was supposed to land a full year earlier than it did, but COVID-19 pushed the release back to November 2021. Given how hands-on the animation process is, with real actors filmed as reference for nearly every scene, a pandemic delay to that kind of workflow makes a lot of sense.

title: The Concept Existed Years Before Production Started
description: Christian Linke and Alex Yee first pitched the idea for a League of Legends show back in the mid-2010s, and Riot's own founders were reportedly hesitant at first since it was a big risk for a game studio. Riot ended up quietly funding concept art and even a test pilot episode in 2016 before the project got the proper greenlight.

title: Fortiche and Riot Went Way Back Before Arcane
description: Long before Arcane existed, Fortiche and Riot were already working together on League music videos, including 'Get Jinxed' and 'Rise' starting around 2013. That earlier working relationship is a big reason Riot trusted Fortiche with something as ambitious as a full TV series years later.

title: There's a Whole Documentary on How It Was Made
description: Riot and Fortiche put out a five-part behind-the-scenes documentary called 'Bridging the Rift', which aired weekly on the League YouTube channel and walked through the entire process from early concept to the global Netflix release.

title: Piltover and Zaun Are Colour-Coded on Purpose
description: The whole visual identity of the show leans on a tightly controlled colour script, with Piltover kept bright, cool and metallic to feel prosperous, while Zaun gets warm, decaying, sickly tones. It's not just pretty to look at, the colour choices are doing a lot of quiet storytelling about class and decay that you might not clock consciously.

title: The Rough Sketch Lines Are a Deliberate Choice
description: Arcane's linework often looks scratchy or uneven rather than perfectly clean, and that's not a technical limitation, it's a specific shader-driven effect the team built to make the animation feel more like a living drawing than a polished cartoon.

title: Vi and Caitlyn Made GLAAD Take Notice
description: The slow-burn romance between Vi and Caitlyn got singled out repeatedly by critics and LGBTQ+ media outlets as some of the most naturally written sapphic representation on TV, developing through body language and shared trust rather than being played for shock value or fan service.

title: Vi's 'Cupcake' Line Was There From the First Draft
description: The moment Vi tells Caitlyn 'you're hot, cupcake' wasn't a late addition, it was in the scripts from the very beginning. The writers fought to keep that line in specifically because it's one of the only times either woman says out loud that she's attracted to the other, rather than leaving it all to subtext.

title: Writer Amanda Overton Worried About Queerbaiting
description: Arcane writer Amanda Overton has said she was genuinely nervous while developing Vi and Caitlyn's relationship, worried the slow burn might read as queerbaiting to fans who've been burned by shows that hint at queer romance without ever committing to it.

title: Arcane Won Best Writing at the Annies for Its Finale
description: Season one's finale, 'The Monster You Created', took home the Annie Award for Best Writing in a TV/Media production, recognising just how much of the season's emotional weight was carried by the script rather than spectacle alone.

title: The Show Held Netflix's Top Spot for Three Weeks Straight
description: Arcane didn't just have a strong opening weekend, it stayed at number one on Netflix's global chart for three consecutive weeks after launch, while also cracking the top 10 in 52 different countries.

title: Arcane Beat Both The Mandalorian and Stranger Things
description: In its third week out, Arcane overtook both Stranger Things and The Mandalorian to become the most-watched streaming show in the US that week, a genuinely surprising result for a video game adaptation nobody was expecting to be a breakout hit.

title: Critics Rated It Higher Than Squid Game at Launch
description: Within a week of its first three episodes dropping, Arcane had a 100% Tomatometer score and a 98% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, edging out Squid Game's numbers at the time and setting the record for Netflix's best-reviewed original series to that point.

title: Arcane Chose Adjustments Over Straight Retcons
description: Some details in Arcane don't line up perfectly with existing League of Legends lore, and creator Christian Linke has been upfront that these aren't meant as retcons. The team saw them as small adjustments made purely to serve the strongest possible story for the show, even if it meant bending a few established facts from the game.

title: Hextech Was Meant to Be an Equaliser, Not a Weapon
description: The whole point of Hextech, as Jayce and Viktor originally envisioned it, was to let regular people without magical talent tap into arcane energy safely. It's the corruption and misuse of that idea, first through Shimmer and later through Viktor's own obsession, that turns a hopeful invention into the thing that nearly destroys both cities.

title: Piltover and Zaun Were Never Meant to Be Equal
description: In the show's own lore, Zaun was originally just Piltover's undercity, a dumping ground for the fumes and waste the surface city didn't want. That founding imbalance, baked in from the start, is really what the entire Piltover-Zaun conflict across both seasons comes back to.

title: Vi and Caitlyn's Romance Was Written Against the Male Gaze
description: Rather than leaning into typical on-screen tropes for female characters, Arcane's writers deliberately shaped Vi and Caitlyn's dynamic around trust and vulnerability instead of spectacle. The show even avoids giving them an on-screen kiss for most of the run, letting small gestures like holding each other's faces carry the weight instead.

title: Silco's Rise Mirrors Zaun's Own History
description: Silco isn't just a random crime boss, his entire arc, clawing his way up from nothing to eventually ruling over Zaun's underworld, is presented as a direct product of the neglect and desperation baked into Zaun's founding. He becomes exactly the kind of ruthless figure that a city built on being ignored ends up producing.

title: The Cast Recorded Together, Not Separately
description: A number of the main cast members, including Ella Purnell and Hailee Steinfeld, have spoken about recording scenes together in the booth rather than each actor doing lines alone. That group approach is part of why sisters Vi and Jinx feel like they have real, lived-in chemistry rather than two separate performances stitched together.

title: Katie Leung Went From Hogwarts to Piltover
description: Caitlyn's voice actor, Katie Leung, is probably best known to a lot of viewers as Cho Chang from the Harry Potter films. Arcane marked a proper return to a major franchise role for her after years working mostly in smaller British TV and theatre projects.

title: The Dragon Language Was Built Around the Theme Song
description: Skyrim's Dragon language, Dovahzul, wasn't planned out as a full language from the start. It was originally created just to give the game's choral theme song, 'Dragonborn,' an ancient, otherworldly sound, and new words were only invented afterward whenever the writers needed to describe something new in-game.

title: The Dragon Language Has No Tenses
description: Senior designer Emil Pagliarulo has explained that as the Dragon language grew, it became too complicated for the design team to use consistently, so verb tenses, conjugation, and apostrophes were dropped altogether to keep it manageable.

title: The Dragon Alphabet Was Designed to Look Clawed
description: According to Game Informer, the written script used for the Dragon language was deliberately designed so its characters looked like they could have been carved by a creature with three front talons and a dewclaw, giving every rune a claw-mark shape.

title: Emil Pagliarulo Voiced 'Fus Ro Dah' Himself
description: Design Director Emil Pagliarulo has said 'Fus Ro Dah' is his favorite shout for its forceful simplicity, and revealed that in Skyrim's reveal trailer, it's actually his own voice yelling it in the recording booth.

title: Max von Sydow Voiced Esbern
description: The late Max von Sydow, known for The Exorcist and The Seventh Seal, lent his voice to Esbern, the elderly chronicler and last living member of the Blades who helps uncover Alduin's return.

title: Christopher Plummer Voiced Arngeir
description: Christopher Plummer, best remembered as Captain von Trapp in The Sound of Music, voiced Arngeir, the Greybeard elder who first teaches the Dragonborn about the Way of the Voice at High Hrothgar.

title: Battlestar Galactica's Colonel Tigh Voiced General Tullius
description: Michael Hogan, recognizable as Colonel Saul Tigh from Battlestar Galactica, provided the voice of General Tullius, the Imperial Legion commander players encounter at the very start of the game in Helgen.

title: The 13th Warrior's Star Voiced Ulfric Stormcloak
description: Vladimir Kulich, who played Buliwyf in The 13th Warrior, voiced Ulfric Stormcloak, the rebel Jarl of Windhelm whose bid for Skyrim's independence drives the game's civil war questline.

title: One Actor Voices Five Different Characters
description: Voice actor Wes Johnson returned to the Elder Scrolls series to voice Sheogorath, Emperor Titus Mede II, the Spectral Assassin, the Wretched Abyss (Hermaeus Mora), and the game's Dremora, plus Hermaeus Mora again in the Dragonborn expansion.

title: Skyrim Sold 3.5 Million Copies in Its First 48 Hours
description: Guinness World Records recognizes Skyrim as the fastest-selling open-world RPG ever, having shifted 3.5 million copies in just 48 hours of release and coming within half a million copies of matching Oblivion's entire lifetime sales inside its first month.

title: Skyrim Has Sold Over 65 Million Copies
description: Bethesda has confirmed Skyrim's lifetime sales have passed 65 million copies across its many re-releases, placing it among the best-selling video games of all time alongside titles like The Witcher 3.

title: Eight People Designed 150 Dungeons
description: Skyrim's dungeon design team consisted of just eight people, who between them were responsible for designing roughly 150 individual dungeons scattered across the game's map, each needing to feel distinct enough to stay interesting.

title: Bethesda Aimed for 'Epic Realism' Over Skyrim's 'Classic' Predecessor
description: The development team designed Skyrim's world around a philosophy they called 'epic-realism,' a deliberate break from what they saw as Oblivion's more generic 'classic' western-fantasy look, aiming for a grounded world with room for stranger, more unique creatures and conflicts.

title: Skyrim Borrowed Design Lessons from Fallout 3
description: Todd Howard told PC Gamer that many of the gameplay changes made since Oblivion were directly inspired by Bethesda's work on Fallout 3, the game the studio released in the years between its two Elder Scrolls titles.

title: The Dragonborn Theme Rhymes in Two Languages at Once
description: Composer Jeremy Soule's choral theme 'Dragonborn' is sung entirely in the fictional Dovahzul language, and its lyrics were crafted so carefully that they rhyme both in the invented Dragon tongue and in their English translation.

title: Paarthurnax Was Alduin's Own Lieutenant
description: Before becoming the peaceful grandmaster of the Greybeards atop the Throat of the World, Paarthurnax served as Alduin's trusted lieutenant during the Dragon War, reportedly committing atrocities against mankind before ultimately betraying his brother and teaching the first mortals the power of the Thu'um.

title: Paarthurnax's Name Literally Means 'Ambition, Overlord, Cruelty'
description: Paarthurnax's name breaks down into three Dragon-language words, Paar, Thur, and Nax, translating to 'Ambition Overlord Cruelty,' a title that reflects the violent history he spent millennia trying to atone for through the Way of the Voice.

title: The Falmer Were Once a Proud, Sighted Civilization
description: The blind, feral Falmer players fight in Skyrim's ruins were once the Snow Elves, a proud and prosperous civilization that rivaled the High Elves before being driven underground by the Nords in the Merethic Era.

title: The Dwemer Blinded the Falmer On Purpose
description: After taking in the defeated Snow Elves as refugees, the Dwemer forced them to eat a toxic fungus as a staple part of their diet, permanently blinding them and their descendants, before enslaving them entirely, ultimately shaping them into the Falmer creatures found underground today.

title: The Dark Brotherhood's Sweetroll Precedes Skyrim by Nearly Two Decades
description: The guard line mocking players about a stolen sweetroll is rooted in a character-creation question going all the way back to 1994's The Elder Scrolls: Arena, where a gang of children demand the player's sweetroll in an alleyway, a scenario that shaped starting stats and later resurfaced across nearly every mainline Elder Scrolls game.

title: Michael Hogan's Character Meets His End Where the Story Begins
description: General Tullius, voiced by Battlestar Galactica's Michael Hogan, is the Imperial commander overseeing the botched execution at Helgen that opens the game, tying the political Civil War storyline directly into the very first cinematic players see when Alduin attacks the keep.

title: Scan Your Way Into a Comic
description: Keep an eye on the walls of the museum where Steven works in episode one — there's a QR code hidden in plain sight, and if you scan it you actually get sent to a free download of Werewolf by Night #32, the comic where Moon Knight made his very first appearance back in the 70s.

title: Gus the Fish Knows the Future
description: Steven's goldfish tank back at his flat is decorated with a tiny pyramid and a little model of Taweret's boat, both of which show up for real later in the season. Given how obsessed Steven is with Egyptology, it makes sense his fish would live somewhere themed to match.

title: A Question That Comes Back to Bite Him
description: Early in episode one, a little girl asks Steven if it hurt when he got rejected from the Field of Reeds. It's such a throwaway moment first time round, but it's actually setting up exactly what happens to him falling from Taweret's boat in episode five.

title: Plushies With a Purpose
description: While working in the gift shop stockroom, Steven hands his coworker Donna a box full of plush toys shaped like the hippo goddess Taweret. It's a blink-and-you-miss-it moment, but it's really the show quietly planting the seed for one of the biggest reveals of the season.

title: The Second Comic Drop
description: Outside Marc's storage unit in episode two, there's yet another scannable QR code, and this one unlocks Werewolf by Night #33 — the second issue Moon Knight ever appeared in, following straight on from the one hidden in episode one.

title: Marc's Passport Has a Familiar Birthday
description: When Steven goes rifling through Marc's storage unit, he pulls out an American passport, and if you pause on it, Marc Spector's birthday is listed as March 9th — which just so happens to be Oscar Isaac's actual birthday in real life.

title: A Case File Number With History
description: When Billy and Bobbi go through their case file on Marc Spector after nabbing Steven, the file's numbered 1975. That's not a random number they picked — it's the year Moon Knight first showed up on the page in Marvel's comics.

title: That Bus Is Doing a Lot of Work
entertainment: The Falcon and the Winter Soldier
description: During the jackal fight at the end of episode two, a double-decker bus rolls past with the number 32 on it (another Werewolf by Night nod) plus an ad for the Global Repatriation Council — the same organisation the Flag Smashers were causing chaos over in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier.

title: Layla's Passport Trick Too
description: Marc's passport isn't the only one playing this game — Layla El-Faouly's passport in episode three lists her birthday as October 28th, which lines up exactly with actress May Calamawy's real birthday.

title: Steven's First Solo Adventure, Hidden in a Hospital
description: There's a QR code tucked away in the asylum in episode five, right next to Steven as he peers through one of the doors. Scan it and it takes you to Moon Knight #1, the character's very first solo comic book.

title: Marc's Bedroom Poster Is Doing Double Duty
description: In young Marc's childhood bedroom during episode five, there's a poster for Star Wars: A New Hope on the wall. It's a nod both to Marc's room in the original comics and a cheeky wink at Oscar Isaac himself, who of course played Poe Dameron in the Star Wars sequel trilogy.

title: Tomb Buster's Hidden Creators
description: That old 'Tomb Buster' movie poster in Marc's bedroom has a name on it, Doug Perlin, which is a mash-up tribute to Doug Moench and Don Perlin, the two guys who actually created Moon Knight for the comics. It even name-drops 'Timely Atlas Studios', a wink at the old publishing names that eventually became Marvel.

title: One Last Comic in the Post-Credits
description: Stick around for the finale's post-credits scene and there's a final QR code that unlocks Moon Knight Annual #1, a comic where he actually squares off against Kang the Conqueror, a character MCU fans had just met via a variant in Loki not long before.

title: Harrow's Ride Home Has a Name
description: In that same post-credits scene, Jake Lockley wheels Arthur Harrow out of a building called Sienkiewicz Psychiatric Hospital. That's a direct tip of the hat to Bill Sienkiewicz, the artist who helped shape Moon Knight's whole look and tone back in the comics.

title: Filming Followed Oscar Isaac to the Desert Again
entertainment: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker
description: Part of the production headed out to the Wadi Rum Desert in Jordan for filming, which happens to be the exact same stretch of desert Oscar Isaac had already shot scenes in for Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker.

title: Budapest Playing Dress-Up as Brixton
description: Rather than shoot on location in south London, the crew found a market street in Budapest and remodelled it, swapping out signage and finding a curved road to mimic Brixton, while a nearby restaurant got dressed up to pass for Soho.

title: That Accent Was Never in the Script
description: Steven Grant's wobbly British accent wasn't written into the scripts at all — head writer Jeremy Slater says the original difference between Steven and Marc was purely down to attitude, until Oscar Isaac pitched giving Steven a distinct voice himself.

title: Nearly Fifty Suits for One Alter Ego
description: Getting Mr. Knight's sharp white suit just right wasn't a one-and-done job — costume designer Meghan Kasperlik and her team ended up tailoring close to four dozen of them over the course of the shoot.

title: An Amadeus Reunion for Khonshu
description: Casting F. Murray Abraham as the voice of Khonshu wasn't a cold call — Oscar Isaac reached out to him personally, since the two had already worked together on the Coen Brothers' Inside Llewyn Davis nearly a decade earlier.

title: Khonshu Had Two Different Actors
description: Khonshu might sound like F. Murray Abraham, but the physical performance you're watching on set was actually captured by Egyptian-American actor Karim El-Hakim, with Abraham's voice layered on afterwards to give the god his commanding tone.

title: Harrow's Bracelets Aren't Just Decoration
description: Arthur Harrow's whole look was built around old cult leader imagery, right down to his rust-coloured linen robe and oversized woven sandals. He also wears two bracelets on screen that are lifted straight from ancient Egyptian art symbolising death.

title: A Week Spent Staring at a Hippo Poster
description: Getting Taweret into the show properly took some stubbornness from showrunner Jeremy Slater, who has said he spent a full week staring at a poster of the goddess in the writers' room before he was fully convinced she needed a proper role and a whole underworld episode built around her.

title: Layla's Transformation Meant Something at Home
description: Director Mohamed Diab has spoken about how personal it was seeing Layla become the MCU's first Egyptian superhero, saying his own daughter used to want to straighten her curly hair because she never saw herself reflected in Disney movies growing up.

title: The Episodes Aren't Quite as Long as They Feel
description: The season isn't made up of even-length episodes — the opener clocks in at 45 minutes while episodes two through four each run 50 to 51 minutes, and all of those times include the roughly 5-minute end credits sequence tacked on.

title: Zilean Is Named After a Real Riot Employee
description: The Chronokeeper's name isn't some deep lore riddle, it's a nod to Tom "Zileas" Cadwell, one of Riot's early design directors. He'd previously worked on Warcraft III and World of Warcraft over at Blizzard before helping shape League's champion roster, so the studio basically named a time-bending sand wizard after their own guy.

title: Fiora Is Named After a 600-Year-Old Fencing Master
description: Fiora's whole fighting style borrows from Fiore dei Liberi, an actual Italian fencing master from the 1400s whose illustrated combat manuscripts are still studied today. Riot didn't just steal the technique either, they basically kept his name too, just swapped a letter.

title: Tristana's Buster Shot Is a Mega Man Homage
description: Look at Tristana's cannon-arm and tell me you don't see it. The little blue-tinged buster shot she fires is a pretty blatant wink at Mega Man's arm cannon, right down to the shape of the blast. Riot's never made a huge deal of it, but once you notice it you can't unsee it.

title: Wait Around After Winning on Howling Abyss
description: Most people hit the victory screen and alt-tab out immediately, which means they miss this one. Stick around on the Howling Abyss for about thirty seconds after a win and Lissandra herself chimes in with a bit of frosty, aristocratic narration about the three sisters. It's a small touch, but it's the kind of thing that makes the map feel less like a leftover and more like its own little story.

title: Singed Was One of the Very First Champions
description: Before League had hundreds of champions, it had four. The mad chemist Singed launched alongside Annie, Sion, and Sivir as part of the original roster, which is a funny thing to think about now that flinging poison in a straight line and running away is still a viable strategy over a decade later.

title: Aatrox Was Built Out of Balrog and Sauron
entertainment: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
description: Senior animator Mike Laygo, who'd previously worked on Lord of the Rings games, has said Aatrox's movement was directly inspired by Balrog and Sauron. It shows too, that same hulking, wing-dragging menace you get from the Balrog in the mines of Moria is baked right into the way Aatrox carries himself.

title: Feed Braum's Poro Enough and It Grows a Moustache
description: Poros are already the most beloved thing Riot has ever made, but there's a bonus if you're playing Braum. Keep feeding your Poro-Snax to the same little critter and it eventually sprouts a big black moustache to match its owner. Purely cosmetic, completely unnecessary, and somehow one of the most-loved details in the game.

title: One Voice Actress Plays Five Different Champions
description: Karen Strassman voices Zyra, Cassiopeia, Fiora, Shyvana, and Elise, five champions who otherwise have almost nothing in common. She's also done plenty of anime voice work on shows like Gurren Lagann and Code Geass, so if any of them sounded oddly familiar, that's why.

title: Zac's Squishing Sounds Were Made With Dog Food
description: According to esports commentator Leigh Smith, the foley team got genuinely gross to nail Zac's wet, gooey sound effects, apparently mixing dog food and beans inside a condom and slapping it against a wall. Disgusting process, but you have to admit the end result sounds exactly right for a living pile of toxic slime.

title: Blitzcrank Moonlights as a Dating Service
description: Dig into the Journal of Justice and you'll find out Blitzcrank isn't just a giant golden robot punching people into the stratosphere, he also runs a chain of magic cafes on the side. The pitch is "Fleshling Compatibility Services," which is Runeterra's oddly clinical way of describing a matchmaking business for champions.

title: Heimerdinger Has Definitely Read Douglas Adams
entertainment: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
description: Yordle inventor Heimerdinger has a line where he mutters "42... there's just something about that number," which is a direct nod to The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, where 42 is famously the answer to life, the universe, and everything. Feels about right for a genius who spends his days building giant turrets out of scrap.

title: The Jaximus Skin Honours a Make-A-Wish Kid
description: The Jaximus skin has a genuinely heartfelt story behind it. It was created to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation after a young patient visiting Riot named Jax as his favourite champion, and every so often Jax will still say "here's to you, kid" as a small tribute to him.

title: The BF Sword Is a Nod to Doom's BFG9000
description: Ever wonder why the plain, unglamorous BF Sword costs so much for a stat stick with no passive? Part of the charm is the name, which is widely taken as a cheeky reference to Doom's ridiculously overpowered BFG9000. Big, expensive, and a little bit of an inside joke.

title: Shaco's Name Is an Anagram of Chaos
description: It sits right there in plain sight until someone points it out to you. Rearrange the letters in Shaco and you get chaos, which is a pretty perfect summary of what it's like to be on the receiving end of his boxes and clones.

title: Jinx Dances Just Like Jake the Dog
description: Someone actually sat down and compared Jinx's dance emote side by side with Jake from Adventure Time doing his own goofy little shuffle, and the moves line up almost beat for beat. Whether it was intentional or a happy coincidence, once you've seen the comparison you can't watch either one the same way again.

title: Vi Started Out as a Roller-Skating Enforcer Named Ruby
description: Before she became the gauntlet-swinging enforcer we know now, Vi's design was completely different. A senior Riot animator revealed her original concept was a roller derby cop named Ruby, patrolling the streets of Zaun on skates rather than punching her way through walls.

title: Kassadin Might Be League's Most-Nerfed Champion
description: Irelia gets a reputation as the champion who's forever getting patched down, but Kassadin's numbers have quietly taken more hits over the years than almost anyone. Cooldowns stretched, damage trimmed, again and again, the poor Void Walker just can't catch a break.

title: Thresh's Starting Souls Depend on Who's in the Lobby
description: Thresh doesn't always start the game with the same number of souls. Queue into a match against Lucian and he kicks off with just one, but there are specific matchup interactions tied to Nunu & Willump and to Sejuani that quietly change his starting count too. Most players never notice the difference, but it's baked right into his kit as a nod to his obsession with Lucian specifically.

title: Riot's Canon Answer for Eating a Poro Is Genuinely Alien-Style
description: Riot has actually gone on record joking about what happens if you eat a Poro, and the answer is somehow worse than you'd expect. Apparently it eats its way back out of your stomach, chestburster style, and if you try to chew one first it just splits apart into several new Poros instead of dying. Cute little furballs, horrifying flavour text.

title: Three Champions Share the Exact Same Voice Actor
description: Draven, Jax, and Vel'Koz all come out of the same voice actor's mouth, which is a genuinely tough one to spot given how different those three characters sound and act. Play their voice lines back to back for someone who's never touched the game and see if they can guess.

title: Winning the Freljord Throne Room Needs a Very Specific Lobby
description: There's a hidden quest called "Leader of the Freljord" that most players will never trigger by accident. You need two of the three Freljordian tribe leaders, Ashe, Lissandra, and Sejuani, on opposite teams in the same game, and winning that specific matchup unlocks a crown as your reward. It's the kind of detail that only really matters to people who've been chasing the last drops of trivia League has to offer.

title: Kalista Fights With the Weapon That Killed Her
description: There's something quietly brutal about Kalista's signature weapon, the Black Spear. According to her backstory it's the very same spear Hecarim used to murder her, and rather than leave it behind she's spent her afterlife as a vengeful spirit wielding it against anyone who breaks an oath.

title: Lux Never Gave Up on Her Injured Horse
description: Lux's horse, Starfire, actually broke a leg at some point in her backstory, the sort of injury that would normally end things for a war horse. Instead of putting the animal down, Lux kept Starfire around anyway, which tells you a fair bit about her character before she ever throws a single light bomb.

title: Nidalee Might Be Borrowed From a French Graphic Novel
description: Riot's never confirmed it outright, but the resemblance is hard to ignore. Nidalee's whole look and vibe, a jungle-dwelling huntress who runs around with a big cat companion, lines up closely with Nävis, a character from the French illustrated series Wake. Coincidence or quiet homage, nobody at Riot has ever really settled the debate.

title: The Black Cleaver's Design Ties It to the Darkin
description: Nobody in Runeterra actually knows where the Black Cleaver came from, but the item's icon is a dead giveaway. It's modelled on Aatrox's own blade, which links it back to the Darkin, the ancient race of fallen ascended warriors who were sealed inside their own weapons after their war nearly destroyed the world.

title: Urf Day Exists Because of a Beloved Boat Captain
description: The yearly Urf celebration on April Fools' Day traces back to a fan-favourite riverboat captain that Riot ended up killing off in the story, and players never really let it go. The whole event doubles as a tribute to him and, a little cheekily, as a reminder of Warwick's animal instincts, since it was his appetite that did Urf in.

title: Tom Cruise Nearly Suited Up
description: Before Robert Downey Jr. ever tried on the suit, Tom Cruise was circling the role back when Iron Man was stuck in development at New Line. Nicolas Cage, a lifelong comic nerd, was also floated at one point. Wild to think how differently the MCU could've kicked off.

title: Downey Turned Up in a Tux
description: Robert Downey Jr. didn't have to screen test given his resume, but he did anyway, and he showed up dressed exactly like Tony Stark would: full tuxedo. It clearly worked, because Marvel handed him the role for a modest $2.5 million, pocket change compared to what he'd later earn.

title: Rhodey Almost Stayed Rhodey Forever
description: Terrence Howard, fresh off an Oscar nomination, was actually the first actor signed to the film and was paid more than anyone else in the cast to play James Rhodes. When he asked for a raise on the sequel, Marvel said no thanks and brought in Don Cheadle instead.

title: There Was Barely a Script
