description: Whimsyshire sounds all bubbly and 8-bit on the surface, but the actual track is Ravel's Gaspard de la Nuit playing backwards. That piece's title translates loosely to 'the Devil of the Night,' so even the silliest level in the game is hiding a joke.

title: The Devs Hid Their Own Names in the Loot Tables
description: Ever picked up Civerb's Vestments and not thought twice about it? Spell 'Civerb' backwards, swap a letter, and you get Brevik, a nod to Diablo co-creators David and Peter Brevik. A bunch of Diablo II's items and locations are staff names in disguise.

title: There's a Whole Dungeon Named After the Dev Team
description: Sometimes the Cemetery of the Forsaken swaps its usual Defiled Crypt for one called Development Hell, and every single monster inside is named after a real Diablo III staff member. You can literally fight lead director Jay Wilson in there.

title: Larry, Curly and Moe Got Turned Into Skeletons
description: After you take down Ezek during the Broken Blade quest, three skeleton guardians show up named Brother Larel, Brother Karel and Brother Moek. Say them out loud and it clicks: it's a goofy little Three Stooges reference tucked into a pretty grim questline.

title: An NFL Team Snuck Into Act II
description: Wander into the Ruined Cistern and you might run into a group of elite Berserkers named after actual New York Giants players, including Jacobs the Gigantic and Bradshaw the Behemoth. No idea who on the dev team was the football fan, but they had fun with it.

title: Nine Toes Becomes Nine Toads
description: There's a rare spawn called Nine Toads, which is a pretty obvious wink at Borderlands' Nine Toes. It doesn't stop at the name either, since killing it can drop a weapon called The Clipper, the exact same name as the gun Nine Toes drops in Borderlands.

title: Boogie Nights in a Dungeon
description: Somewhere in Diablo II's item pool sits a dagger called The Diggler. It's not subtle once you know it, it's a cheeky reference to Dirk Diggler, Mark Wahlberg's character from Paul Thomas Anderson's Boogie Nights.

title: There's a Real Tapestry Hiding in the Cathedral
description: Push through the cathedral late in Act I and you'll pass a wall carving that's actually lifted from the Bayeux Tapestry, the medieval artwork depicting Harold and his knights riding into the Battle of Hastings. Blackly funny place to put it, honestly.

title: Typing 'starcow' Broke the Internet for a Day
description: During the beta, someone found a mysterious empty text box hidden on the Diablo III forums. After a load of guessing, a fan worked out that typing 'starcow' into it unlocked a hidden animation of a cow drifting through space to a Nyan Cat remix. Nobody really knows why it's there, it's just there.

title: Diablo II Almost Didn't Happen
description: Making the first Diablo wrecked the team, so much crunch and so little sleep that by the time it shipped, nobody at Blizzard North was exactly jumping at the chance to start a sequel straight away.

title: The Skills That Got Cut Before Launch
description: An early build of Diablo II had a Necromancer skill that let you take mind control of enemies, and the Druid was meant to be able to shapeshift into an eagle on top of the wolf and bear forms we actually got. Both were scrapped before release.

title: Tyrael Chose to Destroy the Worldstone Himself
description: Once Baal got his claws into the Worldstone and started twisting it to his own ends, Tyrael made the call that nobody wanted to make: shatter it rather than risk Sanctuary falling entirely. It worked, but it also turned Mount Arreat into a smoking crater that was still poisoning the air decades later.

title: Why the Soulstones Exist in the First Place
description: According to the Horadrim monk Jered Cain's own writings, Tyrael gave his order the Soulstones purely to trap the Three Prime Evils. The catch is the stones only pull in non-corporeal spirits, so they were never going to work on anything with a living, breathing body.

title: The Butcher Started Out as an Offhand Joke
description: The story goes that someone on the original dev team looked at an early bloodied-up dungeon room and just said it looked like a butcher's shop. That one throwaway comment is apparently how one of gaming's most feared bosses got his name.

title: His Dying Words Are Actually a Parenting Tip
description: Beat the final boss and listen to his garbled death message played backwards, it comes out as 'eat your vegetables and brush after every meal.' Not exactly the dark prophecy you'd expect from the Lord of Terror.

title: The Butcher Moonlights in Two Other Blizzard Games
description: He's a fully playable melee assassin in Heroes of the Storm, built around a trait literally called Fresh Meat. Over in Overwatch, Roadhog has a Butcher skin, and one of its unique voice lines is, of course, 'Fresh meat!'

title: A Hellraiser Cameo Hiding in Yelesna
description: The side quest 'Unyielding Flesh' has you helping a woman named Krystyna save her husband Feodor, who you find chained up looking a little too pleased with his situation while a mysterious woman hovers nearby. Follow her and things turn very Hellraiser very fast, right down to some of the dialogue.

title: Diablo IV's Class Select Screen Is a Throwback
description: The campfire scene where you pick your class in Diablo IV isn't just a nice bit of atmosphere, it mirrors the layout of Diablo II's own character select screen, right down to where the Druid and Necromancer are standing around the fire.

title: Lara Croft Shows Up as a Dungeon Boss
description: Players dug up an elite enemy inside a Diablo IV dungeon called 'Risen Tomb Raider,' a cheeky little nod to Crystal Dynamics' Rise of the Tomb Raider that's easy to miss if you're not paying attention to enemy names.

title: There's a Secret Crypt Nobody Sends You To
description: South of the Derelict Manor waypoint in Ashwold Cemetery, there's a cracked stone wall that looks like nothing until you get close and see a prompt to 'Enter Hidden Crypt.' It's not tied to any quest, it's just a fully unmarked mini-dungeon with elite enemies guarding a loot chest for anyone curious enough to poke at the scenery.

title: It Shipped on New Year's Eve
description: The original Diablo came out on December 31st, 1996. Releasing a game on the very last day of the year is a weird call by today's standards, but it meant it technically counted as a 1996 release right under the wire.

title: Diablo II Reused a Familiar Tune
description: When you walk back into Tristram in Diablo II, years after the events of the first game, the exact same music from the original Diablo's Tristram plays. It's a small touch, but it hits harder than it has any right to.

title: The Leg You Need to Reach the Cows
description: Remember Wirt, the peg-legged kid who overcharged you for gambling items in the first game? Click his corpse in Diablo II's Tristram and he drops his own severed leg, which you then need alongside a Tome of Town Portal to actually crack open the Secret Cow Level. Grim way to pay tribute to a character, but it works.

title: Wirt's Leg Followed the Devs to Warcraft
description: The Wirt's Leg joke didn't stay contained to Diablo. Over in Warcraft III's Frozen Throne expansion, there's an item called Wirt's Other Leg, and fittingly, it drops from an Abomination that's literally named the Butcher.

title: Even World of Warcraft Has a Third Leg for Wirt
description: By the time World of Warcraft rolled around, Blizzard had turned the whole thing into a running gag across the company. Somewhere in Azeroth there's an item called Wirt's Third Leg, quietly keeping a decades-old Diablo joke alive in a completely different game.

title: Diablo Shows Up as a Sore Loser in a Pod Race
description: Head to Thousand Needles in World of Warcraft and you can stumble into a Star Wars-style pod racing event in the Shimmering Flats. One of the racers is Diablo himself, and he does not look thrilled about being stuck in a go-kart instead of terrorizing Sanctuary.

title: Illidan Wonders If He's Turning Into Diablo
description: One of Illidan's gag quotes in Warcraft III, after he takes on his demonic form, has him muttering 'Wings, horns, hooves... what am I saying, is this Diablo?' A tiny bit of self-aware humor poking fun at how demonic he'd become.

title: Ex-Blizzard Devs Snuck a Wirt Tribute Into Their Own Game
description: When some of the original Blizzard North team left to found Flagship Studios, they clearly couldn't resist bringing a piece of Diablo with them. Their game Hellgate: London includes a quest reward called 'Wart's Peg Leg,' a not-so-subtle parody of Wirt's Leg.

title: A Mysterious Mercenary Name Swap Nobody Explained
description: When Diablo II's patch 1.13 dropped in 2009, fans noticed two mercenary names had quietly changed in the game files, from Weohstan and Erfor to Klar and Tryneus. Blizzard never explained why, and since it happened right as Diablo III was in development, plenty of fans still think it was some kind of quiet lore setup.

title: Someone Made a Rap Out of Deckard Cain's Catchphrase
description: Cain's 'Stay awhile and listen' became so iconic that Blizzard actually had his voice actor, Michael Gough, record a full rap song built around the line. Not something you'd expect from a wise old scholar NPC, but Blizzard leaned into it.

title: Cain's Family Has Been Fighting Diablo for Centuries
description: Deckard Cain isn't just some random old man who happens to know a lot. He's a descendant of Jered Cain, the Horadrim mage who led the original hunt that trapped Diablo and his brothers in Soulstones centuries before the games even start.

title: Cain Doesn't Survive to See Diablo III's Ending
description: After surviving the fall of Tristram and spending years helping heroes across two whole games, Cain finally dies in Diablo III, fatally wounded by the witch Maghda and her Dark Coven while protecting the fallen star that turns out to be Tyrael.

title: The Announcement That Became a Meme Forever
description: When Blizzard revealed Diablo Immortal at BlizzCon 2018, the crowd wanted Diablo IV and let their disappointment be known. A fan asked if it was coming to PC, and the developer's exasperated reply, 'Don't you guys have phones?', instantly became one of gaming's most infamous PR moments.

title: The Expansion Blizzard Didn't Actually Make
description: Hellfire, the only expansion ever released for the original Diablo, wasn't built by Blizzard North at all. It came from Synergistic Software over at Sierra, and Blizzard quietly retconned the whole thing as non-canon not long after it launched.

title: A Guitar Chord Was the Whole Diablo III Reveal
description: Composer Matt Uelmen wrote Diablo's Tristram theme on a 12-string guitar, and it became so recognizable that when Blizzard wanted to announce Diablo III at BlizzCon 2008, all they did was have a guitarist strum the opening chords onstage. Apparently over ten thousand people in the crowd knew exactly what game was coming before a single word was said.

title: A Coin Flip Away From Being Turn-Based
description: Diablo started life as a turn-based dungeon crawler in the vein of Rogue. Creator David Brevik actually fought against switching it to real-time combat, but the studio put it to a vote, he lost, and he ended up reworking the whole system by making turns happen twenty times a second instead.

title: Diablo's Look Was Basically Traced From X-Com
description: When the team needed to figure out how to angle and render their isometric world, Brevik has said he just grabbed a screenshot of X-Com and built Diablo's camera and tile grid to match it exactly, same shape, same size tiles and everything.

title: Diablo Almost Looked Completely Different
description: Before settling on the dark isometric look everyone knows, Diablo was at one point going to be rendered using claymation. It's genuinely hard to picture Tristram's gothic dread working the same way with stop-motion clay models.

title: Only One Book Series Actually Counts
description: Diablo has had a handful of tie-in novels over the years, but according to Blizzard, only Richard A. Knaak's Sin War trilogy is treated as fully canon to the games' story. Everything else sits in a much murkier, semi-official zone.

title: The Man Who Wrote Diablo Also Wrote Half of Azeroth
description: Richard A. Knaak, the author behind most of the Diablo novels, has also written extensively for Warcraft and StarCraft, on top of his own long-running Dragonlance series. The guy clearly doesn't take a day off from world-building.

title: The Novels Take You 3,000 Years Before Diablo
description: The Sin War trilogy isn't set anywhere near the events of the games. It rewinds the clock 3,000 years before the fall of Tristram and follows a farmer named Uldyssian as he gets tangled up in the ancient war between angels and demons over Sanctuary.

title: Tyrael Literally Fell From the Sky as a Star
description: Long before he became a fan-favorite archangel, Tyrael crash-landed on Sanctuary as what looked like a falling star. It was the discovery of his shattered sword El'druin at the impact site that eventually led humanity to uncover the existence of the Nephalem.

title: Every Demon in the Series Comes From One Dragon
description: All seven of the Great Evils, including Diablo himself, were originally born from the seven heads of a single primordial dragon named Tathamet. Three of those heads became the Prime Evils, and the other four became the so-called Lesser Evils.

title: The 'Lesser' Evils Aren't Actually One Family
description: Unlike Diablo, Mephisto and Baal, who consider themselves true brothers, the four Lesser Evils split into two separate pairs. Andariel and Duriel call each other twins, while Belial and Azmodan see themselves as siblings, and that lack of unity is a big part of why the Lesser Evils struggled to team up against the Three.

title: Diablo IV's Big Bad Is Actually Family
description: Lilith, the demon driving most of Diablo IV's story, isn't some new player in Sanctuary's history. She's the daughter of Mephisto, one of the original Three Prime Evils, which makes the whole conflict feel a lot more personal once you know the family tree.

title: The Three Brothers Ruled Hell by Force
description: Mephisto, Baal and Diablo styled themselves as a dark ruling triumvirate over the whole of Hell, using brutal strength and cunning to keep the four Lesser Evils in line beneath them. It's this power imbalance that eventually sparked the rebellion known as the Dark Exile.

title: Diablo Has More Than One Name
description: Outside of the name players know him by, Diablo also goes by al'Diabolos in older Horadric texts, and followers of the Triune sect refer to him as Dialon, the Spirit of Determination. Different cultures in Sanctuary clearly weren't on the same page about what to call the Lord of Terror.

title: Leeroy Jenkins Became Canon
description: That 2005 clip of a paladin charging into a room full of dragon whelps screaming his own name became one of gaming's first proper viral videos, and Blizzard leaned all the way into it. There's now an NPC called Leeroy Jenkins wandering Orgrimmar, plus an achievement that has you re-enact the whole disaster, complete with the 'at least I have chicken' payoff.

title: The Secret Cow Level Made It Into Azeroth
description: Blizzard spent years insisting 'there is no cow level,' a running joke going back to the original Diablo. For Diablo's 20th anniversary they finally caved, at least in WoW: killing a Treasure Goblin in the Broken Isles could pull you into a farmer's field crawling with axe-wielding cows and a boss called the Cow King, who'd hand out a toy guitar that plays Tristram's theme song.

title: Kraes of Immersang, Silvermoon's Self-Proclaimed Prince
description: Wander into Silvermoon City and you might bump into Kraes of Immersang, a troll NPC billed as a self-proclaimed prince. His flavour text piles on every over-the-top backstory cliché roleplay servers are famous for, right down to a throwaway line about fighting a personal war against a random player named Joshua Fuesting. It's Blizzard gently poking fun at its own community.

title: The Undercity's Fight Club Cameo
description: Loiter in the War Quarter of the Undercity and you'll find a small crowd of Forsaken standing around named Chloe Curthas, Tyler, Andrew Hartwell, Robert Gossom and a handful of others. Line the names up and it reads like a cast list for Fight Club, mixing character first names with the actors who played them in the film.

title: Innkeeper Bates and His Motel
description: Tucked away at the Sepulcher in Silverpine Forest is a Forsaken innkeeper who goes by the name Bates. Given that the surrounding zone is dripping with gothic horror atmosphere already, it's hard to believe the Norman Bates nod running the local lodging is a coincidence.

title: Charlie the Unicorn's Cameo in Azsuna
description: Out in Azsuna there's a rare spawn called the Treacherous Stallions, two hostile unicorns standing guard over the corpse of a third. That dead unicorn is simply named Charlie, a direct wink at the cult animated short about a bedraggled unicorn dragged into disturbing adventures, and beating the pair actually rewards you with a kidney.

title: Cloud and Aerith Working Dalaran's Streets
description: Somewhere in Dalaran you can find a flower seller called Aerith Primrose being quietly watched over by her bodyguard, Koraud. Spell it out loud and Koraud is basically Cloud with the letters shuffled, making this pair a sly little Final Fantasy VII reunion nobody asked for but everybody appreciated.

title: Mulgore's Ridiculously Over-Armed Critters
description: On the border between Mulgore and Stonetalon Mountains there's a small plateau populated entirely by oversized mice, rabbits and prairie dogs, all of them decked out with axes, knives and even shotguns, some carrying the skulls of whatever they've already beaten. Nobody's ever gotten a straight answer from Blizzard about why they're there.

title: Blizzard's Own In-House Rock Band
description: Elite Tauren Chieftain isn't just a joke band that shows up in-game, it's a real group made up of actual Blizzard staff, including art director Samwise Didier on vocals and former company president Mike Morhaime on bass. Their song 'Power of the Horde' plays hourly at the Darkmoon Faire, and the band has genuinely performed it live at BlizzCon in full costume.

title: A Kid Once Used WoW to Survive a Real Moose Attack
description: Back in 2010, a twelve-year-old Norwegian boy named Hans Jørgen Olsen ran into an angry moose while out walking with his sister. He taunted the moose to pull its attention away from her, then feigned death once it turned on him, both straight out of his hunter playbook in WoW, and it actually worked; the moose lost interest and wandered off.

title: WoW Was Announced Days Before 9/11
description: Development quietly kicked off back in 1999, but the game wasn't revealed to the world until a European trade show on September 2, 2001, just days before the September 11 attacks reshaped the news cycle. Fans at the reveal were actually expecting an announcement about StarCraft II and were caught completely off guard when Blizzard said it was making an MMO instead.

title: Gnomes and Trolls Almost Didn't Make the Cut
description: Look closely at WoW's original launch cinematic and you'll notice something missing: no gnomes, no trolls. Both races were added so late into alpha development that they never made it into the trailer, long after the other six playable races had already been locked in.

title: Playing WoW Was Linked to Sharper Minds in Seniors
description: A study out of North Carolina State University had a group of 60 to 77 year olds play WoW at home for two weeks after establishing a baseline cognitive score. Those who'd started off with lower scores showed a noticeable improvement in mental agility by the end of it, which is a pretty solid excuse to get your gran into raiding.

title: Bolvar Took the Crown So Nobody Else Had To
description: Once Arthas finally fell at the top of Icecrown Citadel, the Scourge needed a new leader fast or it would've run completely wild across Azeroth with nobody controlling it. That job fell to Bolvar Fordragon, a human paladin badly burned in an earlier battle, who willingly took up the Helm of Domination and became the new Lich King to keep the undead in check from the shadows.

title: The Lich King Has Been Three Different People
description: The Lich King isn't one villain, it's a title that's been passed around. It started with Ner'zhul, an orc shaman whose soul was frozen into a block of ice by the Burning Legion, and it only became Arthas Menethil once the paladin claimed both the cursed runeblade Frostmourne and the Helm of Domination, fusing the two souls into the icon most players remember.

title: Stormwind and Orgrimwar's Guards Went Full Jedi for a Day
description: On the release day of Star Wars: The Force Awakens, city guards in Stormwind and Orgrimmar quietly swapped their usual weapons for glowing blades that looked suspiciously like lightsabers, blue for the Alliance and red for the Horde. It only lasted the one day, so if you weren't logged in you'd have completely missed it.

title: Lunara and Rhonda's Class Hall Cameos
description: The Druid Class Hall in Legion is home to a dryad called Lunara, lifted straight from the MOBA Heroes of the Storm. Wander over to the Monk Class Hall and you'll meet Rhonda, who plenty of players assumed was a nod to MMA fighter Ronda Rousey but is actually named for Rhonda Cox, a real Blizzard sound engineer and martial artist.

title: Once the Biggest Game Wiki on the Internet
description: At its peak, WoWWiki grew to more than 99,800 pages, making it the largest community-run wiki dedicated to any single video game on the internet. That's an enormous amount of collective note-taking from a fanbase that clearly wasn't satisfied with just playing the thing.

title: Jaina's Medallion Looks a Lot Like Scooby's Collar
description: The teleportation trinket you pick up from Icecrown Citadel, Jaina's Medallion, has a shape and colour scheme that lines up suspiciously well with the collar Scooby-Doo wears. Nobody at Blizzard has ever confirmed it outright, but once you notice the resemblance it's genuinely hard to unsee.

title: Kel'Thuzad Used to Be an Ordinary Archmage
description: Long before he was the undead lich guarding Naxxramas, Kel'Thuzad was a respected human archmage and member of Dalaran's Kirin Tor, with genuine standing among the city's magical elite. His obsession with forbidden necromancy got him cast out, and the Lich King's voice found him not long after, turning him into the very first member of the Cult of the Damned.

title: Early WoW Ran on a Modified Warcraft III Engine
description: Because World of Warcraft and Warcraft III were being built at roughly the same time, the two teams ended up leaning on each other. Some of the earliest playable builds of WoW were actually running on a modified version of the Warcraft III engine before the MMO's own tech had caught up.

title: The First Multiplayer Assassin's Creed
description: Brotherhood wasn't just Ezio's second outing in Rome, it was the first time the series let you play against other people. Before this, Assassin's Creed had been a strictly solo affair, so bolting on a full competitive multiplayer mode was a genuine gamble for Ubisoft.

title: A Different Studio Built the Multiplayer
description: The multiplayer side of Brotherhood wasn't handled by the same team that built Ezio's Rome. That fell to Ubisoft Annecy, the studio previously responsible for the multiplayer in Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, and lead designer Arnaud Mametz has talked about the headache of translating a stealth game built for one player into something that worked for a crowd.

title: Fastest Selling Ubisoft Game in Europe
description: Brotherhood shifted a million copies across Europe in under a week, which at the time made it the fastest-selling Ubisoft title the continent had ever seen. Ubisoft's own marketing chief credited the multiplayer mode for turning what had been a single-player brand into something with much broader appeal.

title: A Genuine Speedrunning World Record
description: Frenchman François Federspiel holds the Guinness World Record for completing Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood, clocking in at 2 hours, 23 minutes and 41 seconds back in March 2013. He's since gone on to set similar records for other entries in the series.

title: Over Seven Million Copies Shipped
description: By May 2011, just half a year after launch, Ubisoft confirmed Brotherhood had shipped 7.2 million units, pushing the whole franchise's lifetime shipments up to around 29 million at that point.

title: Lucy's Death Was a Real-Life Pay Dispute
description: There's a reason Lucy Stillman doesn't make it out of Brotherhood alive. Former creative director Patrice Désilets has said Kristen Bell tried to renegotiate her contract for future games, and when a deal couldn't be reached, the writers simply killed her character off instead.

title: One Actor Played Ezio His Whole Life
description: Roger Craig Smith voiced Ezio Auditore continuously from his teenage years at the start of Assassin's Creed II right through to his death at 65 in the short film Assassin's Creed: Embers, giving the character an unusually consistent voice across a good decade of material.

title: Why It Wasn't Called Assassin's Creed III
description: Ubisoft deliberately left this one un-numbered. The team felt fans expected a fresh ancestor and a new setting whenever the number went up, but Brotherhood was really just Ezio's story continuing straight on in Rome, so calling it a sequel rather than a numbered entry made more sense.

title: The Creative Director Left Mid-Development
description: Patrice Désilets, the creative director who'd shaped the series from the start, departed before Brotherhood was even shown off at E3 2010. Ubisoft's line at the time was that he'd simply taken a creative break once his part of the job was finished.

title: Brotherhood Dropped the Always-Online DRM
description: The PC version of Assassin's Creed II had infuriated players by demanding a constant internet connection just to play offline. Ubisoft quietly scrapped that for Brotherhood's PC release, settling for a single login instead, which was a genuine relief for anyone with an unreliable connection.

title: A Writers Guild Award for Its Script
description: Brotherhood didn't just win over players, it picked up a Writers Guild of America award for its story and script, beating out some stiff competition including Fallout: New Vegas and God of War III that year.

title: First Game to Let You Recruit Your Own Assassins
description: Brotherhood was the first entry in the series to let Ezio recruit and train his own roster of assassins, sending them off on missions across Europe. It's a small addition but it's the one that really cemented the idea of Ezio as a leader rather than a lone wolf.

title: The Da Vinci Disappearance DLC
description: Brotherhood's main story DLC, The Da Vinci Disappearance, sees Ezio teaming up once again with his old friend Leonardo after the Templars kidnap him to get their hands on his war machine blueprints. It launched on Xbox 360 in March 2011 before making its way to the other platforms.

title: The Codex Edition's Renaissance Chest
description: Europe, Australia and New Zealand got their own exclusive Codex Edition, packaged inside a Renaissance-styled collector's chest that included a 3D thermoformed portrait of Ezio, exclusive multiplayer characters, bonus singleplayer maps and a DVD of the short film Assassin's Creed: Lineage.

title: Ezio's Story Got Remastered in 2016
description: The Ezio Collection bundled remastered versions of Assassin's Creed II, Brotherhood, and Revelations together for PS4 and Xbox One back in 2016, complete with sharper graphics and every piece of single-player DLC. The multiplayer modes didn't make the cut, though.

title: The Cardboard Box Metal Gear Nod
description: Not long before Ezio reunites with Leonardo da Vinci in Brotherhood, you can stumble across a cardboard box sitting somewhere it really shouldn't be. It's a direct nod to Metal Gear's signature hiding spot, tucked in for anyone paying close enough attention.

title: Rescuing a Princess From Another Castello
description: During the mission 'Femme Fatale', Lucrezia Borgia cracks a joke about Ezio 'rescuing princesses from castles' as he breaks her out of Caterina Sforza's cell, a clear wink at Mario. Ubisoft doubled down on the gag by naming the related achievement 'Principessa in Another Castello.'

title: The Plumber Achievement's Warp Pipe Icon
description: Setting a game in Italy was apparently too good an opportunity to pass up. One of Brotherhood's achievements is literally called 'Plumber', and its icon is a green Warp Pipe lifted straight out of the Super Mario games.

title: Machiavelli's Nod to His Own Book
description: Once you've won over all three faction guilds, you get a short conversation with Niccolò Machiavelli, who asks Ezio how he managed to unite them all. Ezio's answer is a single word, 'virtue', a quiet reference to the ideas Machiavelli laid out in his own famous work, The Prince.

title: "Another Capering Crusader"
description: Climb around Rome's rooftops long enough and you'll eventually hear a passing NPC mutter 'another capering crusader' under their breath. It's a pretty blatant jab at Batman, dropped into a game about a guy who spends most of his time jumping across rooftops in a hood.

title: La Volpe's Bite
description: Brotherhood is full of secret weapons hidden away for players who go looking, and one of the coolest names among them is a blade called 'La Volpe's Bite', tucked away as a reward for anyone thorough enough to track it down.

title: Colosseum Play About the Death of Jesus
description: One of Brotherhood's memories has Ezio disrupting an assassination attempt in the ruins of the Colosseum during a stage play depicting the death of Jesus Christ. Reviewers at the time singled it out as an unusually mature moment for a game about historical stabbing, handled with a lot more care than you'd expect.

title: The 3DS Game That Never Was
description: Revelations almost didn't exist in the form we got. Ubisoft had announced a Nintendo 3DS exclusive called Assassin's Creed: Lost Legacy back at E3 2010, which would've had Ezio travelling to Masyaf to dig into the Holy Land. It got quietly canned a few months later, but the story wasn't wasted, lead writer Darby McDevitt basically took that same premise and folded it straight into Revelations.

title: A New Voice for Subject 16
description: If Subject 16 sounded a little different to you this time round, that's because he was. Cam Clarke voiced him in AC2 and Brotherhood, but for Revelations the North American version swapped him out for Graham Cuthbertson instead.

title: Sofia Was Painted Before She Was Written
description: Ezio's love interest Sofia Sartor wasn't dreamed up from scratch, art director Raphael Lacoste insisted her look come straight from Albrecht Dürer's 1505 portrait 'Portrait of a Young Venetian Woman.' It's a nice bit of circularity, because that very painting shows up as an item you have to retrieve for her during the 'Portrait of a Lady' memory.

title: A Very Cheeky Mission Title
description: One of the story missions is called 'The Spy Who Shunned Me.' Say it out loud and it clicks pretty fast, it's a play on the James Bond film 'The Spy Who Loved Me,' tucked in there for anyone paying attention to the mission list.

title: The Hookblade Started Life as an Upgrade
description: The Hookblade wasn't always meant to be its own weapon. Early on it was pitched as just an add-on for the Hidden Blade, something to bolt onto what Ezio already had. Somewhere in development the idea grew into a standalone item that ended up defining a big chunk of how you move around Constantinople.

title: Faster Feet, Courtesy of the Hook
description: Ubisoft actually put a number on how much the Hookblade sped things up: roughly 30 percent quicker traversal than in the earlier games. Makes sense when you consider Ezio's supposed to be pushing 50 by this point and needs all the help he can get scaling rooftops.

title: Over 300 Ways to Blow Something Up
description: Bomb crafting was the other big new toy in Revelations, and Ubisoft went all in on it. Mix and match the right shells and ingredients and you could theoretically cook up more than 300 different bomb combinations across lethal, tactical and diversion types, though Ezio could only ever carry 15 at a time.

title: Eagle Vision Grows Up Into Eagle Sense
description: The familiar Eagle Vision got a rebrand and an upgrade for this one. Now called Eagle Sense, it let Ezio lock onto a target and get a rough read on where they were headed next, handy if you wanted to sprint ahead and rig an ambush before your mark ever showed up.

title: Built Across Six Studios at Once
description: Just how big a production was Revelations? Big enough that Ubisoft had six different studios working on it simultaneously, a scale that dwarfed anything the series had attempted before it.

title: The Faces Behind Mocam
description: Ubisoft rolled out a new facial animation process for Revelations called Mocam, blending traditional keyframe animation with performance capture. Game Informer likened it to what L.A. Noire was doing, though the side effect was that returning faces like Ezio, Altaïr and especially Desmond looked noticeably different from how players remembered them.

title: Desmond's Coma and the Black Room
description: The framing story picks up right where Brotherhood left Desmond in pieces. After being forced to kill Lucy, he slips into a coma, and the only way to pull him back out is by diving through the Animus into Ezio's memories, which is really the whole reason we're reliving Constantinople in the first place.

title: Assassin's Dens Take Over From the Towers
description: Brotherhood had you burning Borgia Towers to loosen the Templars' grip on Rome. In Revelations that system gets swapped out for Assassin's Dens scattered across Constantinople, each one demanding a different set of objectives before you can flip it to your side.

title: The Spider Assassin Achievement
description: There's an achievement called Spider Assassin that unlocks if you scale the Hagia Sophia in under 25 seconds. The name's not subtle once you notice it, it's a nod to a certain wall-crawling Marvel superhero, following the same trend as the Batman-referencing achievement from AC2.

title: Floats Like a Butterfly, Stings Like a Scorpion
description: Get into a scrap with a citizen or a guard and you might hear onlookers yell 'Floats like a butterfly, stings like a scorpion!' It's a twist on Muhammad Ali's famous description of his own fighting style, swapped just enough to keep it from being a direct quote.

title: We'll Call It a Draw
description: Beat the same brawler three times in the memory 'The Brawler' and he'll grumble 'Ah... we will call it a draw, alright?' That line is lifted almost word for word from the Black Knight in Monty Python and the Holy Grail, who refuses to admit defeat even after losing all his limbs.

title: An Old Trick Resurfaces With Jamal
description: Right after Ezio leaves Masyaf for the first time, there's an Assassin named Jamal standing around who can be silently killed with zero repercussions. It's a deliberate throwback to a nearly identical, consequence-free easter egg buried in the very first Assassin's Creed.

title: Two Composers, One City
description: Jesper Kyd, who'd scored every mainline game up to this point, handled most of the single-player music and leaned into Greek, Renaissance and Middle Eastern instrumentation to match Constantinople's melting-pot setting. Lorne Balfe came in alongside him to write the main theme along with the cutscene and multiplayer music.

title: A Real Orchestra for a Fictional Empire
description: The score wasn't just synths and samples, the Malmö Symphony Orchestra was brought in to actually perform it, giving the Constantinople soundtrack a weight that pure digital instrumentation wouldn't have managed on its own.

title: A Fan's Voice Made It Into the Score
description: Ubisoft ran a public contest called the UJAM Voice of Assassin's Creed Revelations, and the winner, Madeline Bell, actually got her vocals featured on the finished soundtrack. So somewhere in that Constantinople score, you're listening to an ordinary fan who entered a competition and won.

title: Just How Old Is Ezio by Now?
description: It's easy to lose track of time across three games, but Ubisoft has pegged the House of Auditore saga as covering somewhere between 23 and 30 years of Ezio's life, from the hot-headed young noble of AC2 to the tired, world-weary man wrapping up his story in Constantinople.

title: Ezio Turns Up in Some Unexpected Places
description: Ezio's story might wrap up in Revelations, but Ubisoft clearly liked the character enough to lend him out. He showed up as a guest fighter in Soul Calibur V and even had a cameo in the mobile title Academy of Champions: Soccer, of all things.

title: The Mobile Spinoff Told Its Own Story
description: Alongside the console and PC release, Gameloft put out a completely separate Assassin's Creed: Revelations for mobile phones, done up as a 2D side-scroller. It quietly drops Sofia Sartor, Suleiman and Yusuf's death from the story entirely, and even gives Ezio two goes on Leonardo's flying machine, something the main game never lets you do.

title: Fixing an Old Continuity Slip
description: Levantine Assassins are supposed to be missing the ring finger they sacrifice for the Hidden Blade, but the very first Assassin's Creed didn't always bother showing it. Revelations quietly went back and cleaned that detail up, so the animation actually matches the lore this time around.

title: It Started As a Prince of Persia Spin-Off
description: Before it became its own thing, Assassin's Creed was pitched internally as 'Prince of Persia: Assassin', meant to be a spin-off of Sands of Time. The story drifted so far from the Prince that Ubisoft eventually cut it loose to stand on its own two feet.

title: A Master Assassin Who Can't Swim
description: For all his rooftop parkour, Altaïr has one glaring blind spot: water. Jump into a river or the sea and he just sinks, there's no swimming animation in this one at all. Later games quietly fixed this, but the original leaves you stranded if you fall in.

title: Masyaf Castle Is a Real Place
description: Masyaf isn't a made-up stronghold, the castle genuinely exists in northwest Syria and was once held by the real Nizari Ismaili sect. A restoration project between 2000 and 2006 even turned up a hidden underground tunnel and an old bathhouse on site.

title: Al Mualim's Real-World Inspiration
description: Al Mualim is loosely based on Rashid ad-Din Sinan, the real leader of the Hashashin sect in the late 12th century. Ubisoft couldn't use his actual name in the game for legal reasons, so the connection stayed unofficial for years.

title: A Target Who Died at the Wrong Time
description: One of Altaïr's marks, Conrad of Montferrat, really was murdered in history, just not in 1191, the year the game is set. Ubisoft's researchers spotted the mismatch during development and decided the story worked well enough to run with it anyway.

title: Desmond's Face Belonged to a Bartender
description: The model scouted to be the visual basis for Desmond Miles was Francisco Randez, found through an agency search for someone with Mediterranean features. By total coincidence, Randez actually worked as a bartender, exactly like Desmond does before his life gets turned upside down.

title: What Altaïr's Name Actually Means
description: Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad translates roughly to 'the eagle, son of none'. It's not just a cool-sounding name, birds run through the whole series as an Assassin symbol, and 'son of none' nods to Altaïr growing up an orphan, raised entirely by the Brotherhood.

title: The Crossbow That Got Cut
description: A crossbow for ranged kills was in the game at one point, but Ubisoft pulled it before launch. Playtesters were leaning on it too heavily instead of engaging with the melee and stealth systems, and it wasn't historically accurate for the setting either. You can still spot Altaïr wearing one on his back in early trailer footage.

title: Optimus Prime Is Hiding in the Holy Land
description: As an in-joke, the level designers tucked an image of Optimus Prime's face into the architecture of certain buildings, formed by a triple-shuttered window with two boarded-up windows above it. It shows up more than once, across more than one city, if you know to look up.

title: A Finger Sacrificed for the Blade
description: To wield the Hidden Blade, Altaïr had his left ring finger amputated, letting the blade slide cleanly between his other fingers when triggered by a cord-pulled ring. It was both practical engineering and a symbolic rite of passage into the Brotherhood, one later Assassins like Ezio wouldn't have to go through once the design was improved.

title: A Trailer Assassination That Never Happens
description: The game's E3 reveal trailer shows Altaïr crossbow-shooting a bodyguard before assassinating a Templar mid-hanging. None of that scene actually plays out in the finished game, and crossbows weren't even a usable weapon yet, Ubisoft has said the swap was deliberate so the trailer wouldn't spoil real story beats.

title: The Game That Invented Tower Climbing
description: That now-classic open-world habit of climbing a tower to reveal the map and unlock collectibles started right here. Plenty of players found it repetitive even at the time, but it became such a genre staple that even other Ubisoft series like Far Cry and Watch Dogs borrowed it later.

title: A Cast of Mostly Unknown Voices
description: Outside a couple of recognisable names, the voice cast for the original game was made up largely of actors with little to no prior acting experience, a pattern that stuck around for a lot of the series' early entries.

title: Nine Men Stand Between Altaïr and Redemption
description: After Al Mualim strips Altaïr of his rank for a botched mission, he's handed a hit list of nine targets scattered across Damascus, Acre, and Jerusalem to earn his way back into the Brotherhood. Each kill drips out a little more of the game's Templar conspiracy, right up until the reveal that Al Mualim was pulling the strings all along.

title: Over 4,000 Animations for One Assassin
description: Altaïr's movement was built from more than 4,000 individual character animations, an enormous amount for 2007, all in service of making his climbing and parkour feel fluid rather than robotic across the game's rooftops and market stalls.

title: Controls Mapped to Limbs, Not Actions
description: Rather than assigning buttons to specific moves, the original game tied each face button to one of Altaïr's limbs, so the same button could mean climbing, grabbing, or attacking depending on context. It's an unusual scheme the series moved away from almost immediately after this game.

title: PC Players Had to Wait Five Months
description: Assassin's Creed launched on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in November 2007, but PC owners were left waiting until April 2008 to get their own version, a gap that became a fairly common pattern for Ubisoft's console-first releases in that era.

title: Ella Purnell Was Fresh Off Fallout When Jinx Blew Up
description: Jinx's voice actor Ella Purnell had already built a solid resume with Yellowjackets, Army of the Dead and Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children before Arcane, and went on to headline Amazon's Fallout as Lucy MacLean not long after. Jinx is generally seen as the role that really put her on the map for mainstream audiences.

title: Caitlyn's Voice Is Cho Chang From Harry Potter
description: Katie Leung, who plays sharpshooter Caitlyn Kiramman, is probably still best recognised for playing Cho Chang across four Harry Potter films. Arcane gave her a proper lead role again after years spent mostly in smaller British TV and stage work.

title: Viktor's Actor Played Viserys Targaryen
description: Harry Lloyd, who voices the chronically ill genius Viktor, first became widely known playing Viserys Targaryen in the very first season of Game of Thrones. He layers on a distinct accent for Viktor, so it's an easy one to miss unless someone points it out.

title: Jayce's Actor Also Played a Detective on Lucifer
description: Kevin Alejandro, who voices Piltover councilman Jayce Talis, spent years playing Detective Dan Espinoza on Lucifer. He's mentioned in interviews that his own son being a big League of Legends fan played a part in him wanting the role.

title: Vi's Voice Actor Also Voices Gwen Stacy
description: Hailee Steinfeld, who plays the hard-hitting Vi, also lends her voice to Gwen Stacy in the Spider-Verse animated films, on top of her live-action roles as Kate Bishop in Hawkeye and Charlie Watson in Bumblebee. Vi and Gwen Stacy came out in overlapping years, so plenty of fans clocked the voice before checking the credits.

title: Arcane Toppled Squid Game in Under a Week
description: Barely a week after its first three episodes dropped, Arcane had already knocked Squid Game off the number one spot worldwide, taking the top of the chart in 34 countries at once. For a show based on a video game with no prior TV adaptation, that's a genuinely wild launch.

title: Arcane's First Season Beat Out Stranger Things in the US
description: By its second week, Arcane was outpacing both Stranger Things and The Mandalorian as the most in-demand digital streaming series in America, according to audience analytics firm Parrot Analytics, with total demand for the show growing well over 600% in just a couple of weeks.

title: It Landed a 9.4 on IMDb, Rare Company for Netflix
description: Arcane's first season pulled in a 9.4 rating on IMDb, putting it in the same tier as shows like Breaking Bad and Chernobyl, and at the time made it Netflix's highest-rated original series by a noticeable margin.

title: Season 2 Was Already Greenlit Before Season 1 Finished
description: Netflix confirmed a second season was already in production while the finale of season one was still airing, using the tagline 'Ready yourselves, friends' alongside a teaser image of a Hexgate. It's a rare move for a streaming service to commit that early, but the numbers going into that final week made the decision an easy one.

title: A Full League of Legends Spinoff Universe Is Coming
description: Co-creator Christian Linke has confirmed that Riot and Fortiche are already a year into developing the next chapter of the Arcane universe, this time exploring the regions of Noxus, Ionia and Demacia rather than revisiting Piltover and Zaun directly. Riot has since clarified it's not necessarily three separate shows, more a single project exploring those regions, with reports suggesting a late 2026 or early 2027 window.

title: Mel's Noxian Return Was Teased With Its Own Cinematic
description: Shortly after Arcane wrapped, Riot released a League of Legends cinematic called 'Welcome to Noxus' following Mel Medarda heading home to her birth nation, which a lot of fans took as a not-so-subtle hint about where the next show in the franchise might be headed.

title: A Live-Action League Project Has Also Been in the Works
description: Alongside animated spinoff plans, there have been reports of a separate live-action League of Legends TV project, with location scouting reportedly taking place in Vietnam's Cát Bà Archipelago for a planned nine-episode series. It's a completely different production from the Arcane team's animated follow-up.

title: Ekko's Actor Was Told the Role Could Last a Lifetime
description: Reed Shannon, who voices the time-bending rebel Ekko, has said the production team told him this kind of character could end up sticking with him for the rest of his career, given how deep Riot's plans for the wider franchise go beyond just the two seasons already released.

title: Zaun Started Out as Piltover's Dumping Ground
description: According to the show's own lore, Zaun wasn't always its own city, it began life underneath Piltover purely as a place to bury waste and toxic fumes the surface city didn't want dealing with. That original imbalance between the two, baked in from the very start, is what the entire generations-long conflict in the show keeps circling back to.

title: Mel's Power-Up Sets Up Her Noxian Future
description: By the end of season two, Mel Medarda is given a significant magical boost tied to her Noxian bloodline, which lines up with theories that she'll be the connective thread between Arcane and whatever region-based show comes next, given her family ties run straight through Noxus.

title: Viktor's Illness Was the Whole Reason Hextech Existed
description: Viktor grew up chronically ill thanks to conditions in Zaun, and that personal desperation to cure himself is a big part of what pushes him and Jayce toward Hextech in the first place. His arc across the show tracks his slow shift from wanting a cure to wanting something far bigger, eventually pointing toward his fate as the Machine Herald from the games.

title: Ekko's Firelights Live Among Zaun's Last Trees
description: Ekko's crew, the Firelights, are shown living in one of the only pockets of Zaun where actual trees still survive, a small hidden patch of green in an otherwise toxic, industrial city. It's a quiet detail that says a lot about how far Zaun has fallen environmentally without needing a single line of dialogue to explain it.

title: Arcane Was Considered a 'Financial Mess' Behind the Scenes
description: Despite the critical and streaming success, reports emerged that Arcane's budget made it a genuine financial headache internally for Riot Games, reportedly contributing to the company scaling back its wider TV and film ambitions afterward, even as it kept commitments to the Noxus, Ionia and Demacia project alive.

title: Season 1 Almost Lost Out to Squid Game Two Weeks Running
description: For its first two weeks on Netflix, Arcane actually sat at number two worldwide, first behind Squid Game and then behind Hellbound, before finally claiming the top spot outright once its third and final act dropped.

title: Both Seasons Dropped in Three-Episode Acts
description: Rather than dumping a full season at once or doing the usual weekly single-episode drip, Netflix released Arcane in three-episode chunks called Acts, spaced roughly a week apart. It's an unusual middle-ground release strategy that kept people talking between drops without making them wait a full week per episode.

title: Villain and Hero, Same Pose
description: There's a shot of Ivan Vanko hunched over his gear in a grim little garage that's framed almost identically to Tony building his very first suit in the cave back in the original film. It's a nice touch, both men cobbling together something brilliant out of scraps and desperation, just on opposite sides of the law.

title: The Cockatoo Was Mickey Rourke's Idea
description: Rourke didn't want Ivan Vanko to just be a snarling one-note bad guy, so he pitched the idea of giving him a pet cockatoo to soften him up a bit. When he had to fly back for reshoots, Jon Favreau even gifted him his own bird, so there are technically two different cockatoos in the finished film if you look closely at the crest markings.

title: Shoot to Thrill Comes Back in The Avengers
description: The AC/DC track blasting as Tony makes his grand entrance at the Stark Expo is 'Shoot to Thrill,' and Marvel brought it back two years later for the moment Tony faces off with Loki in his tower during The Avengers.

title: The Ironettes Were Real Cheerleaders
description: A chunk of the dancers performing behind Tony at the Expo aren't background extras hired for the day, they're actual members of the LA Chargers cheerleading squad brought in to fill out the routine.

title: Howard Stark's Reel Mirrors a Disney Pitch
description: The old black-and-white film reel of Howard Stark that Tony watches at the Expo is staged very much like Walt Disney's original filmed pitch for EPCOT. A nice bit of irony considering Disney had only just bought Marvel a few months before this movie hit cinemas.

title: Larry Ellison Pops Up Backstage
description: During the chaotic backstage scramble as Tony pushes his way to his car after the Expo, keep an eye out for Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who gets a quick cameo as himself.

title: Stan Lee Gets Mistaken for Larry King
description: Stan Lee's obligatory cameo has him wandering into the backstage crowd, and Tony greets him as though he's talk show legend Larry King, brushing past him without a second thought.

title: Senator Stern Was HYDRA All Along
description: The senator who spends the film trying to strong-arm Tony into handing his armor over to the government turns out, years later in Winter Soldier, to have secretly been working for HYDRA the entire time, which suddenly makes his push for total control over the Iron Man suit feel a lot more sinister.

title: Rhodey's Line Winks at the Recast
description: When Rhodey is dragged in to testify at the Senate hearing, he mutters to Tony that it's him and he's here so just get over it and move on. It reads as a direct nod from the filmmakers to the fact that Don Cheadle had taken over the role from Terrence Howard, basically telling the audience not to make a fuss about it.

title: Tony's Wall Art Nods to the Obama Campaign
description: The poster Tony's eyeing for his workshop wall looks a whole lot like the famous 'Hope' image from the 2008 Obama campaign, which was originally created by artist Shepard Fairey.

title: Jon Favreau Directed and Starred
description: Not content with just calling the shots, Favreau stepped back in front of the camera again as Happy Hogan, Tony's driver turned head of security, a role he'd keep returning to in later MCU films.

title: Christine Everhart Returns from the First Film
description: The Vanity Fair reporter digging into Justin Hammer's business dealings is the same Christine Everhart who interviewed, and later spent the night with, Tony back in the very first Iron Man movie.

title: Elon Musk Chats with Tony in Monaco
description: At the cocktail party before the Monaco race, Tony has a brief exchange with none other than Elon Musk playing himself, years before Musk's own public persona became so tangled up with the real-life Tony Stark comparisons.

title: Hammer's Factory Is Actually SpaceX
description: The sprawling facility used for Justin Hammer's weapons factory is a real SpaceX site, and the crew filmed there at night so that the people wandering around in the background are genuine SpaceX employees going about their jobs.

title: The Suitcase Armor Came from Old Comic Art
description: Tony's slick briefcase-turned-armor was inspired by early Iron Man comic artwork drawn by Bob Layton, who gave the suit a sleeker, more form-fitting look than the bulkier designs that came later.

title: DJ AM's Cameo Became a Tribute
description: The DJ spinning records at Tony's out-of-control birthday party is real-life DJ AM. He passed away from an overdose only months after shooting his scene, and the finished film carries a dedication to his memory.

title: Captain America's Shield Gets an Odd Job
description: You can spot Captain America's shield sitting in Tony's workshop, and rather than treating it like a sacred relic, Tony just slides it under some coils to level them out on his workbench.

title: Wakanda Shows Up on Fury's Map
description: Right near the end of the film there's a map behind Nick Fury marking various locations of interest to SHIELD, and one of the pins sits squarely in the region that would later be revealed as Wakanda.

title: The Thor Post-Credits Scene Wasn't Even Filmed for This Movie
description: That quiet, chilling shot of Coulson finding Mjolnir in the New Mexico crater wasn't shot specifically for Iron Man 2 at all, it was actually filmed on the set of Thor and directed by Kenneth Branagh, not Jon Favreau.

title: Emily Blunt Nearly Played Black Widow
description: Before Scarlett Johansson signed on, Emily Blunt was in serious talks for the Black Widow role but had to bow out because of a scheduling clash with Gulliver's Travels, a film that ended up flopping domestically anyway.

title: Justin Theroux's Only Solo Screenwriting Credit
description: The script is credited entirely to actor Justin Theroux, who's better known these days for The Leftovers. This remains the only film he's ever written completely on his own, though he did share a co-writing credit on Tropic Thunder alongside Robert Downey Jr.

title: A Future Animation Legend Storyboarded the Film
description: The storyboards for the movie were drawn up by Genndy Tartakovsky, the creative mind behind Dexter's Laboratory and Samurai Jack, who'd go on to direct the Hotel Transylvania films.

title: Samuel L. Jackson Signed a Nine-Film Deal
description: Getting Jackson locked in as Nick Fury for another appearance wasn't guaranteed, and the negotiations that followed led to him signing an unprecedented nine-picture deal with Marvel to secure his future in the franchise.

title: Senator Stern Is Named After Howard Stern
description: Garry Shandling's blustering Senator Stern character got his surname as a tip of the hat to radio host Howard Stern, according to Jon Favreau himself.

title: The Monaco Race Was Moved to a California Parking Lot
description: The production originally planned to film the Monaco Grand Prix sequence on location before that year's actual race, but F1 boss Bernie Ecclestone pulled the offer, so the crew ended up building their own racetrack set in a studio parking lot in Downey, California instead.

title: Sam Rockwell Improvised His Dance
description: The little dance Justin Hammer does before showing off his drone army at the Expo wasn't scripted at all, it's something Sam Rockwell does off camera to get himself into character, and Favreau just let the cameras roll.

title: RuneScape's First World Record
description: Back in 2008 Jagex actually picked up a Guinness World Records certificate for RuneScape being the most popular free MMORPG on the planet — and it wasn't even their first time getting it, they'd already held the title the year before. The whole thing got handed over at the Leipzig Games Convention in Germany while they were showing off RuneScape HD.

title: 443 Billion Minutes and Counting
description: As of mid-2012, RuneScape players had collectively burned through 443 billion minutes playing the game. Guinness worked out that's an average of almost 37 hours per account — basically a full working week's worth of grinding for every single person who's ever made a login.

title: The Day the Game Got Rebuilt From Scratch
description: RuneScape 2 dropped on the 29th of March 2004, and it wasn't just a patch — it was a total engine rebuild. The original game got quietly rebranded as 'RuneScape Classic' once the new version took over, and Classic actually stuck around as a legacy option for years after.

title: Prayer Used to Have a Much Creepier Name
description: The Prayer skill wasn't always called Prayer. Early on in development it went by 'Necromancy,' which honestly sounds like a completely different skill tree than the one we ended up with, praying at altars and burying bones.

title: Rune Was Almost a Different Colour Entirely
description: Before Rune armour got its iconic blue sheen, Jagex was reportedly planning to make it purple. Try picturing decades of players grinding for a full purple Rune set instead — it just doesn't hit the same.

title: The Sci-Fi Sequel That Never Happened
description: For a while Jagex was quietly working on a follow-up project codenamed 'MechScape,' aimed at an older audience and built around a sci-fi setting rather than fantasy. It used the same engine tech that powered RuneScape, but the project eventually got shelved and never saw a proper release under that name.

title: Old School Only Exists Because of a Combat Rework
description: Old School RuneScape wasn't part of some grand plan — it exists because players hated the Evolution of Combat update so much that Jagex dug up a backup of the game from 2007 and let people play that version instead. It was meant to be a nostalgia trip, and it ended up becoming its own massively supported game.

title: Classic Finally Got Switched Off
description: RuneScape Classic hung around for way longer than anyone probably expected, but Jagex finally pulled the plug on it for good in August 2018. The official reason was that the ancient codebase was riddled with bugs that were basically impossible to fix without a full rewrite.

title: The Peahat Prank That Upset Partyhat Owners
description: On April Fools' Day 2012, Jagex scattered green Peahats all over the game world for free. It sounds harmless, but a lot of long-time players were genuinely annoyed because the joke item looked close enough to a green partyhat, one of the rarest and most expensive cosmetics in the game, that it threatened to tank their value.

title: The Glitch That Became History
description: The Falador Massacre is one of the most infamous bugs in MMO history. A player called Durial321 found a way to keep attacking people outside PvP zones after being kicked from a house party, and went on a rampage across Falador killing dozens of unarmed players before mods caught up and banned him. Jagex leaned into it years later, actually writing the event into the game's official lore.

title: Durial321 Never Really Left
description: For the tenth anniversary of the Falador Massacre in 2016, Jagex added a little tribute nobody was expecting: log into Falador on the normal servers around that time and there's a chance Durial321's face flashes across your screen for a second before you're handed a green partyhat.

title: Varrock's Library Is Full of Book Spoofs
description: Head to Varrock Palace's library and search the bookshelf in the far north-east corner. Every title on there turns out to be a joke spin on a real-world book, sitting there quietly for anyone who bothers to actually read the shelves instead of just walking past them.

title: A Song With RuneScape Hidden Inside It
description: There's a track called 'Norse Code' in the game's soundtrack, and the flute intro isn't just a nice melody — the notes actually spell out the word 'RuneScape' in Morse code if you know what you're listening for.

title: The War Tortoise Has a Shell-Shocking Secret
description: Examine your familiar War Tortoise closely and you'll spot a pretty blatant Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles reference tucked into its design, which feels like a fun bit of cross-pollination for a summonable pet that's supposed to just be a tank on legs.

title: The Rarest Bird Nest Got Broken by Accident
description: There's a wonky-looking bird nest that's one of the rarest items in the game, and it can't even be obtained normally anymore since the trade route for it got discontinued back in 2016. Years later Jagex tried to give it a proper high alchemy value and instead accidentally updated its x-rotation, so now it just spins weirdly in your inventory.

title: The Bandits Have Opinions About Your Outfit
description: There's a poll booth tucked away in the Bandit Camp, but you can't use it if you're wearing anything with Saradomin's colours on it. The bandits will straight up refuse, telling you they 'don't like your attire' before shooing you off.

title: A Shop Restock That Takes Nearly Five Years
description: The crystal crown sold in the Prifddinas clothing shop is programmed to restock once every 250 million game ticks. Do the maths on that and it works out to roughly 4.8 real-world years between restocks, which is either dedication to detail or a very quiet joke, depending on how you look at it.

title: A Ring That Unlocks a Secret Conversation
description: If you use the Ring of Endurance on the archpriest unicorn found in the Hallowed Sepulchre, it triggers hidden dialogue explaining exactly where the ring actually came from — something you'd never stumble on unless you were pairing two very specific things together for no obvious reason.

title: The Logo Font Moonlights as Restaurant Signage
description: The typeface used for the original RUNESCAPE logo apparently gets reused constantly outside of gaming — it turns up as the signage font for a huge chunk of Asian-themed restaurants across the US, which is a genuinely strange bit of overlap for a font most people associate with a fantasy MMO.

title: There's an Item in the Code You Can Never Get
description: Dig into the old game files and you'll find a 'Life Rune' sitting there in the code — fully defined, but with absolutely no way for players to ever actually get their hands on one. It's basically a ghost item that never made it into the live game.

title: A Definition of 'Underground' That Never Updated
description: Ever notice how some monsters drop nature talismans while others drop chaos ones for seemingly no reason? Monsters in areas the game classifies as 'underground' are supposed to drop chaos talismans, but that classification hasn't been touched since 2003, so it's broken in all sorts of inconsistent ways across the map.

title: Guthix Wasn't Always a God
description: For years the lore treated Guthix as one of the original gods, but it's since been revealed he actually started out mortal and only ascended to godhood by killing another deity, Skargaroth, using an Elder Artefact known as the Blade. Kind of recontextualises the whole 'oldest and most powerful god' reputation once you know he had to earn it the hard way.

title: The Wilderness Used to Be Somebody's Empire
description: Long before it was the lawless PvP zone everyone avoids, the land now called the Wilderness was actually the heart of Zaros's empire, a stretch of Forinthry that spread across huge parts of the map. It only became the wasteland it is today after Zamorak overthrew him and tore the whole region apart in the fighting that followed.

title: The Rules That Kept the Gods Out
description: The Edicts of Guthix get mentioned constantly across quests, but they're not just an ancient law — they're a literal magical barrier Guthix put up after the God Wars to physically stop other gods from setting foot back on Gielinor. It's basically the only reason the world's had any peace at all since he went back to sleep.

title: Where the Tears of Guthix Actually Came From
description: That minigame everyone does for easy experience isn't just a random cave with glowing rocks. According to the lore, Guthix wept over the devastation left behind by the God Wars in a cavern under southern Misthalin, and the surrounding rock supposedly wept with him — which is where the Tears of Guthix are said to actually come from.

title: Sardines Can Get You Out of a Fight
description: During the Fremennik Trials, there's a way to dodge the combat challenge entirely — a bloke called Thorvald will let you skip it if you bring him five sardines. There's even dedicated dialogue for using the sardines on him directly, except it turns out he was just messing with you the whole time.

title: A Cat Broke the Weather Twenty Years Ago
description: Back in 2003, some messy code tied to the Gertrude's Cat quest managed to break the game's 'desert heat' visual effect. Nobody ever went back and fixed it, so as far as anyone can tell, it's just never worked since.

title: Jokes Nobody Will Ever See
description: Scattered through the game's config files there's a bunch of scenery objects with genuinely funny, unique examine text written for them — the only problem is nobody ever actually gave those objects an 'Examine' option, so the jokes just sit there in the code forever, unseen.

title: Nobody's Heard These Villagers Talk Back
description: The level-1 citizens of Miscellania actually have unique overhead dialogue for when they fight back against attackers, but almost nobody's ever seen it. They've only got 1 HP, and killing one costs you 6% of your Miscellania favour, so there's basically no reason anyone would bother provoking them.

title: The Steepest Hill in Gielinor
description: The steepest bit of walkable ground in the entire game is the hill between the waterfall and the Grand Tree — the height value jumps from the absolute lowest possible number straight to the highest in the space of a single tile.

title: A Ladder to Nowhere, Courtesy of 'The Intern'
description: There's a completely inaccessible ladder tucked two floors up in a dark corner of the Smoke Dungeon. The going theory among players is that it's a leftover from an earlier, scrapped version of the Desert Treasure quest, jokingly attributed to a mysterious 'intern' who supposedly worked on it.

title: One Goblin Never Got the Memo
description: There's a single cave goblin miner in the Dorgeshuun mine still using the old, janky pre-2007 goblin chathead model that everyone else moved on from years ago. You have to do something slightly obscure to actually trigger it and see it for yourself.

title: The NPC Who Got Left Behind
description: There used to be an NPC called 'Docky' who ran a boat between Port Khazard and Brimhaven for a small fee. When RuneScape moved from Classic to RS2, Docky himself never made the transition — but strangely, his actual boat did, and it's still sitting there in the game to this day.

title: The 1-in-256 Dialogue Nobody Notices They're Missing
description: The Fremennik NPC who ferries you to Waterbirth Island has a hidden line of dialogue that only fires if your character happens to share the exact same randomly generated Fremennik name as him. The odds of that happening are roughly 1 in 256, so most players will never once trigger it.

title: The Game's Very First Discontinued Item
description: Long before any of the tradeable rares people obsess over today, RuneScape's actual first discontinued item was a random key tied to the Shield of Arrav quest. It only came to light because of an obscure Hungarian RuneScape forum post from 2001 — there's still leftover code for it in OSRS, but a bug means it can never actually run.

title: One Skill Was Too Useless for a Cape Seller
description: When skillcapes launched in 2006, Jagex just needed to find an existing NPC in the right spot to sell each one. That worked fine for 21 of the 22 skills — but one skill was so underused that the devs couldn't find a single fitting character anywhere in the game, and had to invent a brand new NPC purely to sell that cape.

title: Mob Mentality Speeds Up Pyramid Plunder
description: Every time someone starts a round of Pyramid Plunder, the game randomly assigns which tomb door is 'correct' for everyone on that world. Players eventually figured out that if you cram a huge crowd onto one world and get everyone spam-clicking a single door, you basically guarantee someone gets the right one almost instantly.

title: The Satchels That Were Almost Lunchboxes
description: The colourful satchels used in Creature Creation weren't the original plan at all — early versions of the update had them as actual lunchboxes decorated with little animal stickers. For whatever reason, that idea got swapped out for satchels at the very last minute.

title: One Flag Survived a Whole City Rework
description: When Varrock got its 2007 graphical overhaul, every green-and-yellow flag in the city was meant to be swapped for the new colour scheme. They missed exactly one, tucked away in a far corner, and eighteen years later it's still sitting there completely unchanged.

title: Jagex Got Spooked by Their Own Pentagrams
description: Back in 2006, Jagex quietly stripped out all the occult-looking pentagram scenery from the game. They replaced it first with a goofy-looking demon and later with a plain blue blob, and to this day nobody's ever given a clear reason why.

title: Every Monster Was Almost a Wall
description: Those gorilla guards on Ape Atoll that physically block your path aren't a one-off quirk — Jagex originally wanted every single monster in the game to block movement like that, and had to be talked out of it by people pointing out how miserable it would be.

title: A Barrel That Unlocks a Door Miles Away
description: For no clear reason, there's a barrel hidden in the Varrock Sewers that you can search to find a key — and that key opens a completely unrelated door all the way over in West Ardougne.

title: Goblins Who'd Pay Billions for a Potato
description: There's a minigame in Dorgesh-Kaan where you sell exotic food to hungry goblins, and for a while after it launched in 2007 you could offer them something dirt cheap, like a single potato, for a price in the billions. An integer overflow bug meant they'd often just accept it.

title: Coconut Math Checks Out, At Least
description: It's a tiny thing, but a Half Coconut is always priced at exactly half the value of a whole one. In a game full of pricing weirdness and broken drop tables, it's oddly satisfying that this one thing actually does what it says on the tin.

title: Even Your Cat Judges Your Gear Choices
description: Your pet cat isn't just for show — if you wear a dragon chainbody around it, it'll actually talk back with some cheeky dialogue giving you grief about it.

title: The Rarest Weapon You'd Immediately Lose
description: The rune spear in RuneScape Classic might be one of the strangest weapons Jagex ever added. It had roughly a 1-in-a-million drop chance from mid-to-high level monsters, and despite that rarity it was a throwable ranged weapon — meaning you'd permanently lose it the moment you actually used it.

title: The Cheese Glitch Every Ironman Knows About
description: Rat traps scattered around rat-infested areas can be baited with cheese, and other players (or rats) can come along and try to grab that cheese off the trap. Because of how the mechanic works, it's been used as a sneaky way to transfer effectively infinite cheese to an ironman account, which definitely wasn't the intended use.

title: A Wiki Typo That Cost Players a Fortune
description: Thanks to an error on a wiki page, the black shield (h2) ended up trading on the Grand Exchange for roughly ten times its actual worth, and that mistaken price stuck around influencing trades for about three years before anyone properly corrected it.

title: The Runes That Never Made the Cut
description: Most people who've dug through old RuneScape lore know about the mythical Life Rune, but back in 2001 the code briefly also referenced Time, Reality, and Illusion runes. None of them were ever obtainable, and all four were stripped out of the game's code entirely by June of that same year, leaving everyone to wonder what Jagex was originally planning.

title: The Legends' Cape You Could Get on a Brand New Account
description: Back in 2004, there was a genuinely funny exploit where a freshly created account could obtain the Cape of Legends despite Legends' Quest being one of the hardest quests in the game at the time — a loophole players found almost immediately after the quest launched.

title: Announced and Launched in Two Weeks Flat
description: Jagex didn't exactly give players time to get hyped. Dragonwilds went from official announcement to a surprise Early Access launch in just 15 days, which is unusually fast for a spin-off carrying this much weight on its shoulders.

title: It Used to Be Called Aqua Coyote
description: Before anyone outside Jagex knew the name Dragonwilds, the project was running around internally under the placeholder codename 'Aqua Coyote' during its closed Alpha tests.

title: The Project Started Back in 2022
description: Dragonwilds wasn't thrown together to chase the survival-crafting trend overnight. According to a Jagex developer answering community questions on Discord, work on the game actually began in 2022, years before players ever heard about it.

title: It Could Have All Taken Place in the Abyss
description: One of the earliest pitches for the game had the entire adventure set inside the Abyss rather than on a brand new continent. Jagex's Mod Rook confirmed the idea in a community Q&A, though it was dropped so the team could focus the story on Ashenfall instead.

title: Combat Finally Happens in Real Time
description: After decades of RuneScape's click-and-wait combat, Dragonwilds ditches the turn-based system entirely. Players, NPCs and monsters can all swing at the same time, with stamina governing how much attacking and blocking you can actually pull off.

title: The Soundtrack Winks at Old RuneScape
description: Longtime players who keep their headphones on will catch it: Dragonwilds' track 'Harmony' is a direct musical nod to the original RuneScape song of the same name, and Jagex has said more callbacks to both RuneScape and Old School RuneScape's music are planned.

title: An Outside Studio Helped Build the UI
description: Dragonwilds wasn't a solo Jagex effort. Co-development studio Virtuos worked alongside the team to build out the game's UI architecture, including the crafting menus, compass, health and stamina readouts, and the interactive map.

title: The First RuneScape on a Console, Ever
description: In a franchise that's been running for 25 years, Dragonwilds is the very first RuneScape game to make it onto console hardware, landing on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch 2.

title: Straight Onto Game Pass and PS Plus
description: When Dragonwilds hit consoles, it didn't make players pay full price to try it out. It arrived as a Day 1 title on Xbox Game Pass (Premium and Ultimate tiers) and on PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium.

title: Over Half a Million Copies in Week One
description: Jagex CEO Jon Bellamy revealed that Dragonwilds sold more than 600,000 copies in its very first week on Steam, a huge number for a spin-off gambling on a genre already crowded with survival-crafting games.

title: Number One on Steam, Top Three on Twitch
description: During its launch week Dragonwilds climbed to the #1 global top-seller spot on all of Steam and the #3 most-watched game on Twitch, with players averaging more than two hours per play session.

title: A Million Copies Before Christmas
description: By the end of 2025, less than a year after launch, Dragonwilds had crossed one million copies sold, a milestone Jagex used to reveal what was coming next for the game.

title: 1.5 Million Sales Before Leaving Early Access
description: By the time Dragonwilds wrapped up its roughly 18-month stint in Steam Early Access and hit version 1.0 in September 2026, it had sold more than 1.5 million copies.

title: The Land Itself Is Warped by Magic
description: Ashenfall isn't just a pretty backdrop. It's soaked in wild magical energy called anima, and the 'Anima Twist' effect this creates is why you'll find plants glowing in dragonfire colours across the Fractured Plains and other regions looking nothing like the RuneScape you remember.

title: You're Stranded With Some Very Familiar Faces
