description: The expedition team you're stuck with on Ashenfall isn't a cast of nobodies. Slayer Master Vannaka, cave goblin hero Zanik, the Wise Old Man, and dwarf craftsman Doric all show up, each dragging their own RuneScape history along with them.

title: These Goblins Ditched Bandos for a Dragon
description: The goblins roaming Ashenfall used to follow the war god Bandos back in mainline RuneScape lore. On this continent, they've switched allegiance entirely and now serve the dragon general Velgar instead.

title: The Dragon Queen Has Another Name Waiting
description: Kuldra, the Dragon Queen you're working toward all game, picks up a much darker title by the time the story wraps up: in the Scorned Wilderness finale, she's referred to as 'the God Eater'.

title: You Can Chop Trees Without Ever Touching an Axe
description: The game's anima-based magic system lets players summon a spectral axe that fells trees instantly, turning what's normally a slow survival-game grind into a quick bit of casting instead.

title: A Puzzle Where the Password Is Hidden in a Rat's Den
description: During the Highlighting the Problem quest, a glowing blue statue demands a password before it'll do anything. That password, 'pthentorok', is tucked away in a completely different vault, sitting on an elevated ledge in a room full of giant rats, and you don't even need to clear the rest of the vault to grab it.

title: Some Vault Entrances Are Hidden Behind Solid Rock
description: The Fractured Plains Vault won't even show itself until you've dealt with a pile of boulders blocking the way in, which can be cleared with either a pickaxe or the Rocksplosion spell, making it one of the more literal 'hidden entrance' moments in the game.

title: Nobody Wants to Admit Who Invented the Egg
description: Check the in-game description for a regular old Egg and you'll find a surprisingly philosophical bit of flavour text musing over whether chickens evolved or were made by the gods, noting that no god has ever claimed credit for the first chicken or egg, but none of them deny it either.

title: Three New Regions Got Teased Off the Back of a Sales Milestone
description: Right after crossing a million copies sold, Jagex used its community summit stream to reveal three upcoming regions for Ashenfall: Dowdun Reach, Umbral Sands, and Scorned Wilderness, mapping out the rest of the game's ongoing Kuldra Saga storyline.

title: A Chaos God's Fortress Is Full of Corrupted Knights
description: The Dowdun Reach region is built around a long-abandoned mountain fortress under the influence of Zamorak, the God of Chaos, now crawling with corrupted Black Knights and hiding Blue Dragons deeper in its keep.

title: The CEO Wanted It to Earn the RuneScape Name
description: Jagex CEO Jon Bellamy didn't want Dragonwilds to just borrow the RuneScape brand for a quick cash-in. He described it as an entirely new RuneScape experience within Gielinor that had to prove itself 'worthy of wearing the RuneScape name.'

title: Claude's Name Is Never Actually Said Out Loud
description: You'd think the silent protagonist of GTA III would at least get named on screen somewhere, but nope. His name only gets confirmed years later, buried in a phone call you can overhear during San Andreas. Blink and you'll miss it.

title: Banned Down Under
description: Australia actually pulled GTA III from shelves shortly after launch over the violence, and a handful of unedited copies had already made it into people's hands before the ban kicked in. Rockstar had to strip out some sexual content just to get a revised version approved.

title: The Series' First Proper 3D World
description: Before GTA III, the whole series was top-down. This was the game that dragged Liberty City into full 3D, and honestly it's the reason the franchise still exists in the shape it does today.

title: Shooting the Moon With a Sniper Rifle
description: Line up a sniper rifle on the moon and take a shot, and it'll actually change size on screen. Nobody outside Rockstar really knew why this was in there for years, until an ex-developer finally explained it on Twitter.

title: Flashback FM Is Basically the Scarface Soundtrack
description: The playlist on Flashback FM isn't just inspired by Scarface, it's lifted straight from the film's actual soundtrack. When the station came back for Liberty City Stories they swapped it for Giorgio Moroder cuts instead, which makes sense once you remember he scored Scarface in the first place.

title: Random Pedestrians Are Quoting the Village People
description: Wander around long enough and you'll hear civilians drop lines like 'you can sail the seven seas' or 'there's no need to feel down.' They sound like throwaway barks, but they're actually nods to Village People lyrics.

title: The Opening Cutscene Location Doesn't Exist In-Game
description: The bank heist that opens the game takes place somewhere you can never actually walk to during normal play. The only way to even glimpse the area is by getting a Dodo airborne and flying over it.

title: The Series' First Remote Control Car
description: Before RC cars became a recurring bit in later games, GTA III was the one that introduced them to the franchise.

title: The Dodo Was Deliberately Made Rubbish at Flying
description: Rockstar wanted GTA III to be about driving and shooting, full stop, so the only plane in the game was intentionally hobbled. It barely gets off the ground and handles like a brick, because letting players properly fly around wasn't part of the plan.

title: The Dodo Is Technically Coded as a Car
description: Dig into the game's files and the Dodo is classed as a car, not a plane, which explains why it shrugs off crashes like a road vehicle and can even use a handbrake. It's the only aircraft in the whole series with brakes for that exact reason.

title: 8-Ball Almost Had a Totally Different Name
description: Early concept art for 8-Ball labels him as 'Mullan' rather than the name that ended up in the finished game. That name never resurfaced in any later GTA title, so it's just a little fossil from development.

title: A Dreamcast Version That Never Saw Daylight
description: There was genuinely a Dreamcast port in the works at one point, but as the console's fortunes tanked Rockstar shelved it. Because of that, GTA2 remains the only mainline entry ever to reach a Sega system.

title: First Game in the Series to Use Motion Blur
description: Those streaky 'trail' effects you get when sprinting or driving fast made their series debut here, well before it became standard across later entries.

title: Launched the Same Day as GTA2's PS2 Port
description: GTA III hit shelves on the exact same release date as the PlayStation 2 port of GTA2, two years after the original came out. Odd bit of scheduling that meant old and new GTA were sitting on shelves side by side.

title: A Wall-Peeing Cheat That Was Advertised but Broken
description: Some official cheat code books actually printed a code that was supposed to let you urinate on walls. Type it in and, as far as anyone's found, absolutely nothing happens. It just never worked.

title: The Cartoony Art Style That Got Scrapped
description: Liberty City wasn't always going for gritty realism. Early in development the characters moved in a much more exaggerated, childish way and the whole colour palette was way too bright for a gangster story, before the team pulled it back to the tone we ended up getting.

title: The 9/11 Rewrite Rumours Rockstar Always Pushed Back On
description: For years fans insisted the September 11 attacks forced a big last-minute overhaul of GTA III before its October 2001 release. Rockstar has consistently said that's overblown and no major gameplay changes actually happened as a result.

title: Claude Stayed Silent Partly Because of Motion Capture Costs
description: Giving Claude a voice would've meant motion-capturing dialogue at a scale that just wasn't practical back in 2001, so Rockstar kept him mute early on to save themselves the headache. It wasn't until Vice City came around that a talking protagonist was even considered.

title: Ghost Town Names Are a Tribute to the Dev Team
description: Fly a Dodo far enough north past Shoreside Vale and your radar starts showing place names for towns that don't physically exist anywhere in the game. Turns out those names are all references to real Rockstar staff who worked on the title.

title: 'You Weren't Supposed to Be Able to Get Here'
description: There's a wall in a Bedford Point alleyway you're not meant to reach without glitching over it or using a Dodo, and if you do get there, a sign is waiting to call you out for it directly.

title: A Billboard That Spoiled the Next Game
description: Somewhere in Liberty City there's a billboard cheekily reading 'See you in Miami!' It's a straightforward tease for Vice City, dropped in well before anyone outside Rockstar knew where the next game was headed.

title: Darkel, the Cut Mission-Giver
description: GTA III originally had a character called Darkel who'd hand you missions built around blowing up buildings with bombs. He got dropped before launch, likely for being a bit too close to real-world terrorism given the timing, but he's still listed in the manual with his voice actor credited and his model is sitting untouched in the game's files.

title: K-JAH's Peaceful DJ Took Over From His Cousin
entertainment: Grand Theft Auto: Liberty City Stories
description: Horace Walsh, better known on air as 'the Pacifist,' spends his K-JAH broadcasts begging Liberty City to put the guns down and lay off the SPANK. His backstory actually stretches back to Liberty City Stories, where his cousin Natalie was running the station before he eventually took her spot.

title: Game FM's Hosts Were Real Hip-Hop DJs Playing Themselves
description: Game FM wasn't voiced by actors doing a bit, it was hosted by actual New York DJs Stretch Armstrong and Lord Sear playing versions of themselves, banter and all. It gave the station a completely different feel from the rest of Liberty City's more parody-heavy radio lineup.

title: One of Game FM's Real DJs Passed Away in 2026
description: Steve Watson, the New York DJ known as Lord Sear who co-hosted Game FM back in 2001, died in March 2026 at 53. For a lot of players his voice was inseparable from cruising round Liberty City, since Game FM leaned into genuine East Coast underground hip-hop rather than the parody stations elsewhere on the dial.

title: Every GTA III Radio Station Runs on One Repeating Loop
description: None of the nine stations shuffle their playlists. Every song, ad break and DJ line plays in the exact same order every single time you tune in, which is part of why long-time players can still recite the ad breaks from memory.

title: The Actual Easter Egg
description: Rockstar's sense of humour is very literal sometimes. Down near the VCN building in Downtown there's a window you can jump through, and inside is a proper brown chocolate easter egg, sat on its own little pedestal like it's the most important artefact in the game. It does nothing. It's just there because the joke was too good to pass up.

title: Reagan and Gorbachev on the Firing Range
description: There's a hidden poster you're not meant to see properly, tucked inside the Ammu-Nation in the northern part of the second island. Grab a rocket launcher, aim it at the right wall and the camera clips through, showing Ronald Reagan giving a thumbs up next to a bullet-riddled Mikhail Gorbachev. A weirdly specific bit of Cold War humour for a game about jet skis and mob bosses.

title: Cement Shoes, Vice City Style
description: Dotted around the coastline are a couple of unlucky souls sitting on the seabed with their feet set in concrete blocks, the classic mob way of making someone disappear for good. One's off the coast near Washington Street, the other near Skumole Shack. Nobody in Vice City is filing a missing persons report about either of them.

title: Apartment 3C
description: Find the right building and you can climb up to a specific apartment that's just soaked in Scarface references, blood-stained bathroom, chainsaw and all. It's a straight nod to the film's infamous scene, and it's a little unsettling how much care went into recreating something so grim in a game that otherwise plays its violence for laughs.

title: The Romero Family's Side Businesses
description: Wander through Little Haiti and you'll find the Romero Family Funeral Home sitting right next to Romero Family Butchers, which is exactly as morbid as it sounds once you look closer. There's a tombstone in the funeral parlour window naming a real level designer from the team, and round the back there's an unmarked grave and a skeleton. The butchers next door has a box labelled human organs and an arm resting among the cuts of meat. Subtle it is not.

title: The Mansion With the Rude Pool
description: There's a mansion on Starfish Island with a swimming pool that looks completely normal from ground level. Get up high enough to look straight down on it though, and the pool's shape plus the rocks at the bottom form the unmistakable outline of a woman's torso in a bikini. Somebody on the art team clearly had fun with that one and knew most players would never bother checking from above.

title: A Poster for an Old Friend
description: Tommy's room at the Ocean View Hotel has a poster on the wall featuring Claude, the silent protagonist from GTA III, even though Claude himself didn't actually have a name yet at this point in the series and wouldn't be seen in Vice City itself since the story is set fifteen years earlier. A small tip of the hat from one game to the one that came after it.

title: Every Car Shares One Number Plate
description: Look closely at any vehicle you steal and you'll notice every single one is running the same plate, VC R29. It's a little detail that carried over the series' habit from GTA III, where every car in Liberty City read LC R29 instead. Nobody in Vice City seems bothered by the obvious paperwork fraud.

title: The Missing AK-47
description: Vice City is the odd one out in the whole 3D-era run of GTA games for not letting you carry an AK-47, a weapon that shows up in basically every other title including its own prequel, Vice City Stories. Digging through the game's files shows references to the gun that never made it into the final build, so it looks like it was planned and quietly dropped somewhere along the way.

title: It Started as a GTA III Add-On
description: Vice City wasn't originally meant to be its own game at all. After porting GTA III to PC, Rockstar started kicking around the idea of a mission pack that would bolt some new weapons, vehicles and missions onto Liberty City. The concept just kept growing until it made more sense as a standalone release, and that's how we ended up with an entirely new city instead of a glorified expansion pack.

title: It Was Almost Called GTA Miami
description: Early on, the plan was to set the sequel in the real city of Miami and call it exactly that, GTA Miami. Somewhere along the way Rockstar decided a fictional stand-in gave them more freedom, so they built Vice City instead and pushed the timeline back to 1986, well before the events of GTA III.

title: Built in Nine Months
description: Full production on Vice City reportedly only lasted around nine months, which is a genuinely wild timeline for a game of this scale even by today's standards, let alone 2002. The team leaned heavily on assets and tech already built for GTA III to hit that deadline, and it clearly paid off given how the game turned out.

title: The First Fully Voiced GTA Protagonist
description: Tommy Vercetti was a proper turning point for the series since he was the first GTA protagonist to actually talk, voiced by Goodfellas star Ray Liotta. Before that, series heroes like Claude in GTA III were completely silent, so giving the lead a real personality and a Hollywood name attached to it was a big deal at the time.

title: Burt Reynolds Nearly Threw Hands in the Booth
description: Recording sessions weren't always smooth sailing. Burt Reynolds, who plays wealthy businessman Avery Carrington, reportedly got so irritated by Dan Houser hanging around during his session that things nearly turned physical between the two of them. Reynolds ended up delivering a great performance anyway, but it says something that Rockstar mostly moved away from big-name actors after GTA IV.

title: Phil Cassidy Keeps Turning Up
description: Phil Cassidy, the one-armed gun nut voiced by Gary Busey, isn't just a one-off mission giver here, he's one of the more persistent faces across the whole 3D Universe, popping up again in later GTA titles set on the same timeline. For a guy who mostly just sells you weapons and blows things up, he's earned an oddly loyal following.

title: Sharks Swimming Beneath the Surface
description: Vice City's waters actually have sharks patrolling underneath, though most people never clock them because the water's murky enough to hide the detail. They're far more visible in the original PS2 release than on later remasters, where the clearer water almost works against the secret. They don't attack you, they're just quietly there.

title: The PC Version Leaked Onto Shelves Early
description: The Windows release accidentally ended up on shop shelves a full five days before its official street date, and once that got out plenty of other retailers just started selling their copies early too rather than sit on stock while customers next door were already playing. A logistics slip that basically fixed itself.

title: Germany Got Extra Songs
description: Thanks to some licensing headaches in the US, the German release of the game actually shipped with more radio tracks on it than the American version got. It's a strange little quirk of music rights that meant not every player was hearing quite the same soundtrack, depending on where they bought the game.

title: Why Tommy Never Learned to Swim
description: Fall in the water in Vice City and Tommy just sinks, no swimming animation, no rescue, just a quick death. Rockstar addressed it directly in an interview with PSM2 at the time, basically saying that programming proper swimming would have taken too long and that watching a hardened gangster paddle around wouldn't have looked especially cool anyway. Swimming didn't actually arrive in the series until San Andreas.

title: Lance Vance Is Basically Tubbs on Vacation
description: Lance Vance is voiced by Philip Michael Thomas, who spent the 80s playing Detective Ricardo Tubbs on Miami Vice, the exact show Vice City is riffing on wholesale. Thomas liked the role enough that he came back to voice Lance again years later in the prequel, Vice City Stories, so the connection clearly wasn't lost on him either.

title: 100 Packages, One Tank
description: Hunting down every one of the game's 100 hidden packages scattered across the map isn't just a completionist badge of honour, it actually unlocks a Rhino tank at Tommy's properties once you've found the lot. Considering how tucked away some of these packages are, that reward feels well and truly earned by the time you get there.

title: A City Named After Its Own Inspiration
description: The name Vice City is doing double duty, it's obviously winking at Miami Vice, the neon cop show the whole aesthetic is lifted from, but it's also just a literal description of the place. A city built almost entirely on drugs, corruption and greed genuinely earns the word vice without needing the TV reference at all.

title: Toni Cipriani's Radio Career Follows Her
description: DJ Toni on Flash FM is the same Toni Cipriani who ran Flashback FM back in GTA III, just younger and considerably more naive this time round given Vice City's earlier timeline. A chunk of her on-air material even reuses jokes from her GTA III stint, including the bit about her having been on fire, which is a nice bit of continuity for anyone who remembers the earlier game.

title: Fernando's Radio Days
description: Long before Fernando Martinez was running his euphemistically named prostitution ring, Fernando's New Beginnings, he actually got his start on the airwaves as a DJ on Emotion 98.3. He's already dropping hints of his future pimping ambitions between songs, which is a fun little breadcrumb for anyone who bothers listening closely to the in-game radio.

title: The $10 Million Gamble
description: Back in 2004, San Andreas reportedly cost around $10 million to make, and that's before marketing was even factored in. Sounds tiny by today's standards, but for the time it was one of the most ambitious budgets in gaming.

title: A Sequel Built in Record Time
description: San Andreas launched just two years after Vice City, yet it packed in a map several times bigger, around 100 story missions, and a mountain of side content. For a Rockstar team working on that timeline, it's honestly kind of wild.

title: CJ's Actor Never Left the Family
description: Young Maylay, the rapper who voiced CJ, never played the character again, but he stuck around Rockstar's orbit. He went on to host the West Coast Classics radio station in GTA V and even popped up in the Contract DLC.

title: The Bonus Prequel Nobody Talks About
description: The special edition PS2 release and the official soundtrack CD came with a bonus DVD containing a short film called The Introduction, built in the game's own engine. It quietly sets up plot threads that pay off later in San Fierro and Las Venturas.

title: The Girlfriend Missions That Almost Went Further
description: During development, Rockstar apparently planned a flirtier mini-game for CJ's dates, something closer to a rhythm challenge where you'd tap keys to build up the mood. It got scaled back before release, though echoes of the idea stuck around in the finished dating system.

title: The Gant Bridge's Practical Joke
description: Wander to the area around the Gant Bridge and you'll find an in-game sign listing goofy 'bridge facts' about the crossing between San Fierro and Las Venturas. It's a tiny detail most players speed straight past without ever reading.

title: A Guinness-Certified Giant
description: As of 2008, Guinness World Records recognized San Andreas as having both the largest in-game soundtrack and the largest voice cast of any video game up to that point. It held the soundtrack crown until GTA IV came along with 218 licensed tracks to San Andreas's 156.

title: Banned Down Under
description: When the Hot Coffee content came to light, Australia's Attorney-General opened an investigation, and on 29 July 2005 the game actually lost its rating entirely, meaning it couldn't legally be sold there. Rockstar had to submit a cleaned-up version a few months later to get it back on shelves.

title: The Search for Bigfoot
description: Almost as soon as the game launched, players convinced themselves Bigfoot was hiding somewhere in the countryside near Back o' Beyond, and the rumor refused to die for years. Rockstar's own co-founder eventually shot it down publicly, though that didn't stop people from combing the woods with in-game cameras looking for him.

title: A German Comedy Sketch Took a Shot at It
description: San Andreas got spoofed in an episode of Die Redaktion, a monthly comedy segment made by the German gaming magazine GameStar, which shipped on the DVD bundled with one of their 2005 issues. A funny little reminder of how far the game's cultural footprint reached.

title: The Horse Race Roster Has Jokes
description: In the horse racing mini-game, one entrant is literally named 'Henrik's Jaw,' a nod to Celtic striker Henrik Larsson breaking his jaw around the time the game was in development. Sitting right next to it on the roster is a horse cheekily named after the Scotland national team's habit of crashing out of tournaments early, a joke that only really lands if you know Rockstar North is based in Scotland.

title: The Multiple Protagonist Idea That Came Too Soon
description: Rockstar toyed with letting players switch between multiple playable characters way back during San Andreas, but the hardware of the era just couldn't handle it. The idea got shelved for nearly a decade until GTA V finally pulled it off with Michael, Franklin, and Trevor.

title: Real Streets Became Real Textures
description: The art team photographed real Los Angeles neighborhoods extensively during development, and a lot of those photos ended up baked directly into the game's textures. Halfway through production the New York studio even went back to double-check every reference to keep the recreation accurate.

title: DJ Pooh Was the Studio's Street Connection
description: Producer and writer DJ Pooh personally drove Rockstar's team around Los Angeles to soak up the culture that shaped the game's early-90s setting. One voice actor later described him as the crew's direct line to the people who actually lived that world.

title: Franklin's Actor Had a Cameo Years Before GTA V
description: Long before Shawn Fonteno became the voice and face of Franklin Clinton in GTA V, he already had a foot in the door on San Andreas, voicing a recruitable gang member called Fam1 and a handful of other background characters.

title: Not Every Bridge Is the Golden Gate
description: Everyone assumes the Gant Bridge is a Golden Gate clone, and it is, but the Garver Bridge over in the same area is actually modeled on the Forth Road Bridge near Edinburgh. Makes sense once you remember a big chunk of the dev team was working out of Scotland.

title: The State's Name Is a Geology Joke
description: San Andreas takes its name straight from the real San Andreas Fault, the earthquake-prone line running through California that the game's fictional state sits on. Rockstar even wove it into the world itself, with San Fierro showing quake damage and in-game news reports referencing tremors.

title: The Mod That Nearly Sank Rockstar
description: In June 2005, a Dutch modder found a disabled sex scene still sitting in the game's files and released a fix to switch it back on, calling it Hot Coffee. It spread fast, and within weeks Rockstar was staring down a full-blown industry crisis rather than just a modding curiosity.

title: Hot Coffee Reached the US Senate
description: The fallout from Hot Coffee got so big that the ESRB stripped the game's rating, major retailers pulled it entirely, and Senator Hillary Clinton pushed legislation targeting the games industry off the back of it. Rockstar eventually patched the content out for good, a fix fans nicknamed 'Cold Coffee.'

title: Samuel L. Jackson Played the Bad Cop
description: One of San Andreas's biggest casting coups was landing Samuel L. Jackson to voice Officer Frank Tenpenny, the corrupt cop who hounds CJ through most of the story. Oddly enough, Jackson has barely ever spoken publicly about taking the role.

title: Tenpenny Was Ripped From the Headlines
description: Frank Tenpenny's character is widely believed to be modeled on Rafael Perez, the real LAPD officer at the center of the Rampart corruption scandal, right down to a passing resemblance to another officer implicated alongside him. It gives the story's villain an uncomfortable grounding in something that actually happened.

title: Ryder's Voice Actor Was a West Coast Rap Legend
description: MC Eiht, frontman of Compton's Most Wanted, lent his voice to Ryder, the unpredictable Grove Street member who ends up betraying the crew. Fittingly, Ryder's look is widely thought to be inspired by the late Eazy-E.

title: Ice-T Played a Rapper on the Skids
description: Gangsta rap pioneer Ice-T voiced Madd Dogg, the fading rap star whose career CJ accidentally wrecks early on before eventually helping put back together. It's a nice bit of stunt casting, given Ice-T basically lived through the era the character is parodying.

title: The Game That Made CJ Get in Shape
description: San Andreas was the first game in the series to give its protagonist actual RPG-style body stats, letting CJ bulk up, slim down, or let himself go depending on how the player fed and exercised him. It's a system the series never fully brought back in later entries.

title: Fifty Oysters for a Better Lung
description: Scattered across the map are fifty collectible oysters, and hunting down every single one doesn't just unlock an achievement-style reward, it also maxes out CJ's lung capacity and sex appeal stats in one go. A nice payoff for the kind of completionist who checks every rock along the coastline.

title: Guns Get Better the More You Use Them
description: San Andreas quietly introduced a weapon proficiency system, where sticking with the same gun over time made CJ noticeably more accurate and stable with it. It's the kind of mechanic that later open-world games leaned on heavily, but San Andreas had it running back in 2004.

title: A Map Four Times the Size
description: San Andreas's map dwarfed everything the series had done before, packing in three full cities and twelve smaller towns across roughly 17 square miles of countryside. It was, by a wide margin, the biggest playground GTA had ever built up to that point.

title: DJ Pooh Discovered CJ's Voice
description: According to DJ Pooh himself, it was his encouragement that got his friend Young Maylay to audition for the role of CJ in the first place. He talked about it years later, crediting his own enthusiasm for the series as part of what pushed his friends toward Rockstar.

title: The Name Nearly Wasn't Modern Warfare
description: Before they landed on the name we all know, Infinity Ward reportedly went through well over a thousand potential titles for the game. Some of the rejected ones were properly daft too, including the frankly brilliant Call of Duty: Warnado.

title: Shipment Was Never Meant to Ship
description: One of the most beloved multiplayer maps in the whole franchise only exists because somebody forgot to delete it. Multiplayer design director Geoff Smith has said Shipment started life as an internal test map built for old-school split-screen play, and it got accidentally left in the launch playlist. Nobody ever pulled it back out.

title: A Rude Number Plate Hidden in Vacant
description: Take a wander round the outside area on the multiplayer map Vacant and you'll spot a parked truck. Zoom in on its number plate and it reads 'Я3T4ЯD0', which if you squint is just a backwards spelling of a certain playground insult.

title: An Airplane! Tribute Hidden in Mile High Club
description: The loading screen for the bonus mission Mile High Club quietly nods to the 1980 comedy Airplane!. Listen closely as it loads and you'll hear one voice ask 'Surely you can't be serious?', followed by the classic reply, 'I am serious, and don't call me Shirley.'

title: Germany Got a Softer Cut
description: The German release trimmed the blood out of the sniper mission One Shot, One Kill and dropped the arcade mode entirely. Even the on-screen word for headshot got swapped, changed from the English term to 'Volltreffer', which just means direct hit.

title: The Nuke Was Built to Make You Feel Powerless
description: That gut-punch of a scene where Sergeant Paul Jackson crawls out of a downed helicopter into a mushroom cloud wasn't just there for shock value. Critics have pointed out it deliberately strips away every bit of control the campaign spent hours building up, right before killing the character off outright, which is almost unheard of for a genre built on power fantasies.

title: Soap Didn't Actually Speak in His Debut
description: Sergeant 'Soap' MacTavish is one of the series' most recognisable faces now, but in his very first appearance he was a silent protagonist. He didn't get an actual voice actor until Modern Warfare 2 came along.

title: A Chernobyl Timeline Clue Hidden in Dialogue
description: During the flashback mission, Captain Price mentions the events are happening a decade after the Chernobyl disaster. Do the maths on that and it quietly places the whole flashback in 1996, years before the rest of the campaign takes place.

title: Captain Price Was Played by a Soap Star
description: Long before he was barking orders in the SAS, Billy Murray, the voice behind Captain Price in the original trilogy, spent years playing Don Beech on The Bill and later Johnny Allen on EastEnders. He stuck with the role of Price all the way through the first three games.

title: Price Got Recast Because of His Age
description: When the series rebooted in 2019, Barry Sloane took over as Price instead of Billy Murray. Part of the reasoning reportedly came down to Murray being 77 at the time, which made the heavy motion capture work the newer games demand a much tougher ask.

title: A Wink at Its Own Cut Content
description: In the training mission F.N.G., if you retry the CQB test and start doing worse, Captain Price grumbles that maybe it was a mistake letting you skip the obstacle course. Funny thing is, there really was a much larger obstacle course planned for that mission before it got cut, so the line is basically a joke about content that never made it in.

title: Some Cut Multiplayer Maps Turned Up Later Anyway
description: Not every map made it to launch. A pair called Favela and Invasion were cut from Call of Duty 4's Variety Map Pack, but Infinity Ward clearly didn't want to waste the work, because both eventually resurfaced in Modern Warfare 2 instead.

title: Night Versions of the Maps Almost Existed
description: Digging through old build files shows Infinity Ward experimented with night-time versions of several multiplayer maps, including Ambush, Strike, District and Overgrown. They were basically identical to the day versions bar the lighting, and none of them made the final cut.

title: It Killed Off the WWII Shooter for a While
description: Before 2007, 'generic shooter setting' basically meant World War II. Call of Duty 4 flipped that overnight, and the shift was so complete that even other long-running WWII franchises started scrambling to set their games in the modern day instead.

title: It Set the Template Every Shooter Still Copies
description: The perk system, killstreaks, and customisable loadouts that feel completely standard in shooters today all trace back to this game. It's been copied so thoroughly by other studios that it's now considered unusual for a modern shooter not to have some version of it.

title: One Actor Voiced Two Different Soldiers
description: Craig Fairbrass pulled double duty on this one, voicing both Gaz and a character called Wallcroft, before going on to become a very different fan favourite as Ghost in Modern Warfare 2.

title: Banned Outright in Two Countries
description: The game never made it onto shelves in Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates, where it was banned over its depiction of violence against Islamic soldiers.

title: The Face on the Box Art Is a Real Developer
description: That soldier staring out from the cover isn't a stock model or an actor. It's actually Mark Rubin, who worked at Infinity Ward at the time.

title: No Trophies at Launch on PS3
description: PlayStation 3 owners picking this up at launch wouldn't have found a single trophy to earn. Sony's trophy system simply hadn't been built into the platform yet when the game shipped.

title: Grandma's House Made a Comeback in Warzone
description: Long-time players will remember the riverside house on Overgrown, the one with a climbable roof and a machine gun tucked in the attic, affectionately nicknamed 'grandma's house' by the community for reasons nobody can quite agree on. That same house was quietly rebuilt inside Verdansk when Warzone launched.

title: Vacant Is Hiding Inside Verdansk
description: Vacant got its own full multiplayer remake eventually, but a chunk of the original map is also tucked away near Port on the Verdansk map in Warzone, for anyone who fancies a nostalgic detour.

title: It Made the '1001 Video Games' List
description: This one picked up a spot in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die, putting it alongside decades of games considered essential playing.

title: It Got Name-Dropped in The Wrestler
description: Darren Aronofsky's 2008 film The Wrestler has a scene where a kid explains the game to Randy 'The Ram' Robinson while they're playing a fictional title on an old console together, a nice little nod to how big it had become in pop culture by then.

title: It Showed Up in Kick-Ass Too
description: The game gets a proper appearance in the 2010 film Kick-Ass, another sign of how quickly it became shorthand for gaming culture at the time.

title: It's the Reason We All Say 'Noob Tube'
description: The phrase existed in smaller gaming circles before this game came out, tracing back to Halo 2 forums as far back as 2004. But it was Call of Duty 4's underslung grenade launcher that pushed the term into the mainstream and made it a permanent part of shooter slang.

title: The Shipping Containers Sign Their Own Work
description: Head to any multiplayer map with the big shipping containers, Shipment is the easiest spot, and take a proper look at the white lettering stencilled on the sides. Depending on the container, it reads out as 'INFINITY WRD' or 'COD MW', a sly little signature from the studio itself.

title: The Dentist's Chair
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: In one of the very first rooms of Nacht der Untoten there's an old dentist's chair just sitting there. Hold the action button on the wheel at its base and you'll hear the drill start up along with a man screaming. Nobody needed that in a zombie survival map but here we are.

title: Flush The Toilet Three Times
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: One of the more bizarre hidden songs in Nacht der Untoten, 'Lullaby for a Dead Man,' only plays if you flush one of the toilets in the map three times. Treyarch clearly had some spare hours to burn on this one.

title: Dial the Phone, Hear 'The One'
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Head to the hut with the Comm Room section and dial the telephone three times and you'll trigger a hidden song called 'The One.' It's the sort of thing you'd never stumble on without a guide, which is half the fun.

title: The 115 Song
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Activate all three pieces of the meteor scattered around Nacht der Untoten and the map rewards you with a hidden track called '115' - named after the fictional element that basically drives the entire Zombies storyline going forward.

title: The Giant Cow of Crossroads
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Tucked away in a hidden room on the Crossroads map (from the United Offensive-style content) is a giant cow, which most people reckon is a cheeky nod to Saturday Night Live's 'More Cowbell' sketch. Very random, very Treyarch.

title: The Hidden Snowman
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: On The Russian, there's a snowman wedged between two trees that most players run straight past without noticing. It's not exactly hard to find once you know it's there, but blink and you'll miss it mid-firefight.

title: Free Ray Gun in Little Resistance
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Right at the start of Little Resistance there are three puddles along the beach. Stand in each one for about ten seconds, working your way along, and staring at a palm tree by the last one triggers a fake 'earthquake' followed by Japanese statues rising up holding a Ray Gun for you to grab. Great way to farm points if you're playing co-op.

title: The Meteorite Outside the Map
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Walk past the little shed in the Storage area of Nacht der Untoten and look out past the barriers - there's a big red meteorite just sitting out there beyond the playable space. It ties back to the whole 115/meteor lore thread that runs through Zombies.

title: The Three (or Four) Gun Trick
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: There's a long-known Zombies exploit where you grab a Mystery Box weapon while still mid-animation drinking a Perk-a-Cola, letting you carry three guns instead of two. Get downed while holding a live grenade, get revived, and repeat the trick to stack even more. It's fiddly but people were doing it for years before it got patched out in later titles.

title: It Was Almost Called Call of Duty V
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Before settling on World at War, Treyarch and Activision were reportedly planning to just call this one Call of Duty V, keeping the numbered naming from the earlier games going. Glad they didn't - 'World at War' has aged a lot better as a title.

title: Headshots Don't Stop the Screaming
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Shoot an enemy's head clean off in this game and they'll still let out a scream, despite very obviously no longer having the equipment to do so. A weird little audio bug that nobody at Treyarch seems to have caught before shipping.

title: Wet Screen, Fake Glasses
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Get caught out in the rain or wade through water and you'll sometimes see little droplets appear on the screen, as if your character was wearing glasses rather than, you know, having eyes exposed to the elements like a normal soldier.

title: Veteran Difficulty Doesn't Like Campers
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Hang around too long without progressing an objective and the game starts lobbing grenades at you constantly - it's especially brutal on Veteran difficulty and is basically Treyarch's way of telling you to stop hiding behind that crate and push forward.

title: The British Campaign That Never Was
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: A whole British campaign was planned for World at War at one point, and you can still find unused weapons like the Sten, Bren and Lee-Enfield sitting dormant in the game files. There were even three cut missions set in Holland that survived into the Mod Tools. Would've been a very different game.

title: Pvt. Pyle's Full Metal Jacket Nod
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: In the opening mission you run into a soldier named Pvt. Pyle - a direct wink at the character from Full Metal Jacket, right down to sharing the 'Gomer Pyle' nickname. Subtle enough that plenty of players never clock it.

title: Saving Pvt. Ryan (Again)
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Partway through the first level you're tasked with saving a Pvt. Ryan, which is about as unsubtle a Saving Private Ryan reference as you can get. World War II shooters just can't resist bringing him up.

title: The Only CoD Without the British
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
Call of Duty: World at War – Final Fronts
description: As of when it launched, World at War was the only mainline Call of Duty to not feature British forces at all, focusing purely on the US and Soviet fronts instead. They did sneak back in on the PS2/Wii spin-off Final Fronts though, where they actually replaced the Russians entirely.

title: A 15 Rating for the Bloodiest Entry Yet
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Despite having some of the most graphic violence and by far the most swearing of any Call of Duty game up to that point, World at War somehow got away with a BBFC 15 rating in the UK, while most other entries in the series landed a PEGI 18.

title: Gary Oldman and Kiefer Sutherland Lead the Voice Cast
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Sgt. Reznov is voiced by Gary Oldman and Sgt. Roebuck by Kiefer Sutherland - a proper stacked cast for a 2008 shooter. Reznov went on to become one of the most memorable characters in the whole Call of Duty series thanks largely to Oldman's performance.

title: 13 Death Cards Hidden Throughout the Campaign
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Scattered across the campaign are 13 collectible Death Cards, usually tucked near fallen soldiers or fixed to makeshift graves. Find one and it unlocks a co-op cheat, like paintball bullets or enemies that never drop weapons - track down all of them and there's an achievement waiting for you too.

title: Nazi Zombies Started Out as a Joke
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: The entire Zombies mode wasn't originally meant to be a big deal - it began life as a bit of a throwaway joke mode inside Treyarch, only unlocking once you'd beaten the campaign. Nobody expected it to become the thing the studio is arguably best known for now.

title: Nacht der Untoten Was a Secret Nobody Announced
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Nacht der Untoten - German for 'Night of the Undead' - wasn't advertised anywhere before launch. Treyarch just quietly hid it behind the campaign's final mission, so early players stumbled into the very first Zombies map with zero warning about what it even was.

title: Shi No Numa Introduces the Original Crew
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Shi No Numa is where Tank Dempsey, Nikolai Belinski, Takeo Masaki and Edward Richtofen first show up together as the playable four-man crew - a lineup that would go on to anchor the Zombies storyline for years across Black Ops and beyond.

title: The Asylum's Ghostly Sounds
entertainment: Call of Duty: World at War
description: Stand in the right spot on the multiplayer map Asylum and you can pick up faint piano music, ghostly whispering, and even the sound of dogs barking somewhere in the distance. It's easy to write off as background noise unless you're specifically listening for it.

title: The 11-10-09 Countdown
description: The marketing team had a bit of fun with the release date. Every trailer leading up to launch flashed the date as '11-10-09', with the numbers ticking on one by one like a countdown to a detonation. Cute touch for a game about a world going up in flames.

title: Biggest Entertainment Launch Ever
description: MW2 didn't just beat other games at launch, it beat every form of entertainment period. It pulled in $310 million across the US and UK in its first 24 hours, blowing past Grand Theft Auto IV's previous record and beating out music and film releases too.

title: 4.7 Million Copies Before Breakfast
description: Roughly 4.7 million copies flew off shelves worldwide in the first day alone. By March 2010 that number had ballooned to over 14 million, making it the second best-selling game ever in the UK at the time and third in the US.

title: Hans Zimmer's Video Game Debut
description: Before he was scoring Dune and Dark Knight sequels, Hans Zimmer wrote his very first video game score for MW2. You can hear that cinematic, dread-heavy sound all over the campaign's big set pieces.

title: Remember, No Russian
description: Right before the airport massacre kicks off, Makarov mutters 'С нами Бог' (God is with us) then tells his men in English: 'Remember... no Russian.' It's not just a creepy line, it's the whole plan. Keep the gunmen speaking English so the attack gets pinned on America instead of him, which is exactly the spark that sets off World War III for the rest of the game.

title: Pulled From Shelves in Russia
description: The airport massacre mission caused enough of a stir that Russia yanked the level entirely, releasing the game there with it stripped out completely. Other regions got softer treatment, but Russia just cut it loose.

title: Shoot a Civilian, Get a Game Over
description: Japan and Germany didn't get the mission cut, but they did get it rewired. In those versions, if you actually fire on the civilians during 'No Russian' instead of just walking through it, the game slaps you with an instant Game Over screen.

title: The Gamestation 5 in the Mansion
description: Head into the big house on the Estate multiplayer map and check the rack underneath the TV in the main hall. There's a console sat there called a 'Gamestation 5', a cheeky PlayStation dig, with a couple of games next to it: 'Italian Plumber Princess Rescue' and 'Deer Hunter 17'. Not exactly subtle, but funny every time.

title: License Plates With a Hidden Credit
description: Some of the car license plates scattered around the game read 'IW20094'. Break it down and it's Infinity Ward's own signature: IW for the studio, 2009 for the year it came out, and 4 marking it as the fourth game they'd built.

title: The 1337 Train
description: On the multiplayer map Derail there's a blue freight train engine sat on the tracks. Take a look at the number painted on its side and you'll spot 1337, a little wink to the old internet slang for 'elite'.

title: MW2 Never Die
description: At the end of the campaign mission Exodus, you're meant to grab a briefcase and move on. Skip it and drop prone instead, and if you look closely you'll spot two scraps of paper lying nearby that both read 'MW2 Never Die', a little goodbye note from the devs.

title: A Stash Hidden in the Garden
description: On the campaign level The Hornet's Nest, break away from the main path and head right, then cut through a shack tucked near some barrels. Keep pushing and you'll end up in a small garden with a stash of items waiting at the far wall, if you know where to turn.

title: The Boss Fight That Got Cut
description: General Shepherd was originally meant to go out in a proper boss fight staged on a version of the Rust map, but it got swapped for a simpler scripted cutscene before launch. If you pay attention during the actual ending, Rust is still sitting there visible in the background, a leftover trace of the fight that never made the cut.

title: Raptor Was Almost the President
description: Digging through the game's files shows that Raptor, the VIP you pull out during the Wolverines! mission, was originally written to be the President of the United States. That got dialled back before release, but the finished game still leaves heavy hints that he's someone seriously high up.

title: The One Mainline Game That Skipped the Wii
description: Every other mainline Call of Duty between Call of Duty 3 and Modern Warfare 3 got a Wii release. MW2 is the odd one out, Nintendo owners were handed a port of Call of Duty 4 instead of the actual sequel.

title: 25 Kills, One Nuke
description: MW2 is where the Tactical Nuke killstreak was born. String together 25 kills without dying and you could call one in, ending the match on the spot with your team taking the win while a mushroom cloud filled the screen. It became the single most bragged-about achievement in the whole series.

title: The Firing That Sparked Respawn
description: Barely months after MW2 turned into one of the biggest launches ever, Activision fired Infinity Ward's own founders, Jason West and Vince Zampella, citing insubordination. The pair fired back with a lawsuit claiming they were dumped right before a huge royalty payout was due. It eventually settled out of court, but not before West and Zampella had already gone off and started Respawn Entertainment.

title: 38 Developers Also Sued Activision
description: The fallout from MW2's success didn't stop at the top. A group of 38 current and former Infinity Ward staff filed their own lawsuit, arguing Activision had only handed out $28 million of a $118 million bonus pool tied to the game's sales and kept the rest.

title: Rust Never Really Left
entertainment: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II (2022)
description: Rust, the tiny industrial 1v1 map everyone spent hundreds of hours dueling on back in 2009, quietly resurfaced over a decade later. Head to the B flag on the Taraq map in the 2022 Modern Warfare 2's Ground War mode and you'll find an almost identical structure sitting there as a nod to where it all started.

title: Burger Town Never Closed
description: You fight through a Burger Town restaurant during the Wolverines! mission in the original 2009 campaign. That same fictional chain has kept popping up in later Call of Duty releases, including a sign spotted on the Verdansk map, a running gag that all traces back to this one throwaway location.

title: Far Cry 3's Nod to Task Force 141
description: MW2 was big enough that rival studios started referencing it. In Far Cry 3, a character named Willis Huntley casually mentions he's 'flying out to Russia with Task Force 141', borrowing the exact name of Soap and Price's elite unit for a quick joke.

title: Battlefield Took a Swing at MW2's Heartbeat Sensor
description: Not every studio was flattering about it though. In Battlefield: Bad Company 2, a character named Sweetwater mocks the idea of calling in backup by griping they'll just send 'special ops douchebags with pussy-ass heartbeat monitors on their guns', a pretty direct dig at MW2's signature gadget.

title: The Menu Room Has a Working Text Adventure Hidden Inside It
description: Before you even hit start on the campaign, you're strapped to a chair being interrogated. Rock the triggers back and forth fast enough and you break free, wander over to the terminal in the corner, and can type in a bunch of commands. One of them just loads up Zork, the 1977 text adventure Activision happens to own the rights to, complete with its own achievement for getting eaten by a Grue. It's a proper, playable version too, not some stripped-down tribute.

title: That Same Terminal Unlocks an Entire Arcade Shooter
description: Once you're loose from the interrogation chair, typing DOA into the CIA terminal drops a full top-down zombie shooter called Dead Ops Arcade into your Zombies menu. It plays like a twin-stick Smash TV knockoff, and getting through the opening sequence just to reach it was such a rite of passage that later ports kept the exact same trigger-mashing intro untouched.

title: Nuketown's Mailboxes Are a Quiet Nod to Its Own Hero
description: Walk up to the two houses on Nuketown and you'll notice the mailboxes are stamped with the names Mason and Woods, the two characters you spend the campaign playing alongside. Flip into spectator mode and cross to the far side of the barbed wire fence and there are even more mailboxes with names nobody's fully pinned down, suggesting Treyarch dressed the whole set more than most players ever bothered to check.

title: Nuketown's Population Sign Actually Counts You
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: That faded 'Welcome to Nuketown' billboard isn't just set dressing. The population number on it genuinely changes to match how many players are currently in your match. It's such a tiny detail most people never look up long enough to notice, but Treyarch carried the idea forward, giving it an actual gameplay job as a kill counter in the Black Ops II zombies version of the map.

title: There's a Doomsday Clock Ticking Just Outside the Map
description: Nuketown is tiny, but its makers still snuck a detail past the map's own boundaries. If you go into spectator mode and pan the camera out, there's a clock tower sitting off in the distance that's actually a doomsday clock, counting down toward the end of the round rather than any real time of day.

title: The Whole Campaign Twist Hinges on a Man Who's Already Dead
description: For most of the game you fight alongside Viktor Reznov, the gruff Russian soldier who's been dragging Alex Mason toward revenge since World at War. The big reveal near the end flips that entirely: Reznov actually died early in the story, and every appearance after that point was Mason's own fractured mind keeping him around, a side effect of the brainwashing Reznov himself had tampered with.

title: Shooting Reznov Gives You a Different Response Depending on When You Do It
description: Normally the game scolds you and resets the checkpoint the instant you turn a gun on an ally, and Reznov is no exception, at least at first. Players eventually noticed that shooting him during his introduction in Vorkuta gets the usual 'you betrayed your comrades' warning, but doing it in any of his later appearances triggers different dialogue entirely, a subtle nod to the fact he isn't really there anymore.

title: Reznov's Father Fought in the Same Battle He Did
description: During the mission Project Nova, Reznov mentions in passing that his own father was present at the Battle of Stalingrad, the same fight Reznov himself survived back in World at War. It's a blink-and-you'll-miss-it line, but it adds a whole extra generation to a character whose backstory already carries most of the game's emotional weight.

title: Mason Has Apparently Been Dressing Like Reznov the Whole Time
description: Pay attention during the Rebirth Island mission and you'll notice Reznov is wearing the exact same outfit as Mason. It ties into the reveal that Mason believed, on some level, that he actually was Reznov, and it's a nice bit of visual foreshadowing that only really clicks once you already know the twist and go back looking for it.

title: Reznov's Dog Tags Turn Up in a Sequel He's Barely In
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Even though Reznov's role in Black Ops II is little more than a cameo, his dog tags are still obtainable as a collectible reward in the Kill Confirmed multiplayer mode. It's the kind of thing only die-hard fans of the character would ever bother chasing down, but it's a nice bit of continuity for a character who barely appears in the sequel's story.

title: Reznov's Voice Actor Has Played Real Cold War Figures Before
description: Viktor Reznov is voiced by Gary Oldman, and according to GamesRadar's rundown of the game's cast, he's just one part of a genuinely stacked lineup that also included Ed Harris as Hudson and Ice Cube as Bowman. Oldman's other credits stretch from JFK to Christopher Nolan's Batman films, which makes his gravelly Soviet soldier feel almost understated by comparison.

title: A Bunch of Horror Icons Play Themselves in the Zombies DLC
description: The Call of the Dead zombies map didn't bother inventing new characters for its cast. Danny Trejo, Robert Englund, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and Michael Rooker all show up playing themselves, complete with motion capture, turning the map into a strange little horror convention where the guest stars are also the ones fighting off the undead.

title: The Director of Night of the Living Dead Plays the Zombie Boss
description: As if stacking a zombies map with horror actors wasn't enough, Treyarch also brought in George Romero, the filmmaker who more or less invented the modern zombie movie, to play Call of the Dead's undead antagonist. It's a fittingly on-the-nose casting choice for a map that's already dripping with genre homage.

title: Batman Took Over as Jason Hudson's Voice
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: When Jason Hudson returns for Black Ops II, he's no longer voiced by the same actor from the first game. Michael Keaton stepped into the role instead, giving Hudson a new voice years after Keaton had already played his own version of Batman in Tim Burton's films.

title: Two Real Political Figures Show Up as Themselves in Black Ops II
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Former Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega and retired Marine lieutenant colonel Oliver North, of Iran-Contra fame, both appear in Black Ops II's campaign, with North voicing his own character. It's a strange bit of casting even by Call of Duty's usual standards, mixing real-world figures with controversial pasts directly into the fiction.

title: Jimmy Kimmel Hosts a Fake Late-Night Show Inside the Game
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Black Ops II's epilogue features Jimmy Kimmel playing himself, hosting a fictional episode of his own talk show within the game's near-future setting. It doubles as some pretty shameless self-promotion on Kimmel's part, but it fits right in with the game's habit of blending real celebrities into its 2025 vision of the world.

title: A Real Four-Star General Becomes Secretary of Defense in the Game's Future
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Black Ops II cast retired general David Petraeus as the Secretary of Defense in its 2025 storyline, serving under a fictional female president aboard a carrier named the USS Barack Obama. The timing was almost unbelievably awkward, since the game launched the same week Petraeus resigned as CIA director over an extramarital affair in real life.

title: A Real Defense Analyst Helped Design Black Ops II's Future War
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: To make its 2025 setting feel plausible rather than pure sci-fi, Treyarch brought in writer and defense analyst P.W. Singer, who handed developers a list of emerging military technologies sorted by how close they actually were to real deployment. That's part of why so many of the game's drones and cyberwarfare elements ended up feeling less like fantasy and more like an early preview of where things were actually heading.

title: You Meet JFK in Person, Twelve Days Before He's Assassinated
description: During the campaign mission U.S.D.D., President Kennedy personally briefs Mason at the Pentagon and greenlights the mission to take down Dragovich. The story then jumps forward less than two weeks to Kennedy's trip to Dallas, and the final cutscene quietly places Mason himself in the crowd that day, leaving it deliberately unclear whether his brainwashing ever really got switched off.

title: JFK Is a Playable Character If You Know Where to Look
description: Kennedy isn't just a campaign cameo. He's one of the four playable characters in the zombies map Five, using a different, more exaggerated voice actor than his campaign appearance. On the map Ascension, there's also a ringing telephone you can pick up to hear him shout a line about needing 'some beans for the chowder,' a strange little callback that has nothing to do with the plot but has stuck with fans for years anyway.

title: Black Ops Sold Faster Than Any Entertainment Release Before It
description: On its first day alone, Black Ops moved roughly 5.6 million copies across North America and the UK, pulling in about $360 million and beating the previous record set a year earlier by Modern Warfare 2. Activision called it the biggest entertainment launch in history at the time, and for a while nothing else in games, film, or publishing had come close.

title: The Game Hit a Billion Dollars in Under Six Weeks
description: By late December 2010, barely six weeks after launch, Activision announced Black Ops had crossed a billion dollars in worldwide sales. Players had also logged more than 600 million hours in the game by that point, with the average person reportedly playing for over an hour every time they sat down with it.

title: Cold War's Hero Isn't Who the Game Tells You He Is
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: For most of Black Ops Cold War, you play as an operative named Bell, working alongside Adler's CIA team. Late in the story it comes out that Bell's entire backstory was implanted, and he was really a Russian operative working for the antagonist Perseus all along, a twist the game leans into pretty hard once your character starts remembering things that don't match the identity you'd been given.

title: One Interrogation Choice Decides Which of Three Endings You Get
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: Despite all the choices scattered through the campaign, Black Ops Cold War really only has one moment that matters for its ending: whether you tell Adler the truth about Perseus hiding at the Solovetsky Monastery, or lie and send the team to Duga instead. Telling the truth leads to the canonical good ending, while lying opens up two darker variations depending on what you do afterward.

title: Shooting Every Mannequin's Head Off Unlocks a Secret Retro Filter
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: When Nuketown '84 launched for Cold War, fans quickly worked out that shooting the heads off every single mannequin scattered around the map triggers a hidden visual effect, dropping the whole screen into a green or purple-and-blue retro filter reminiscent of old arcade cabinets. It's a small touch, but it ties in nicely with the map's 80s setting and the game's love of arcade-era references.

title: There's a Character Hiding in Nuketown Zombies' Backyard Shelter
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: In the Black Ops II zombies version of Nuketown, if you walk up to the fallout shelter door in the yellow house's backyard and knife the door, you'll hear Marlton Johnson, a character from the TranZit storyline, muttering complaints from inside about the dust and radiation. He's not doing anything else on the map, he's just stuck in there, reusing lines from a completely different level.

title: Shoot Every Mannequin's Head Off in Time and Nuketown Plays You a Rolling Stones Song
description: Nuketown is dotted with mannequins standing around in the yards, and if you and your team manage to headshot every single one within about fifteen seconds, the map rewards you by blasting 'Sympathy for the Devil' over the loudspeakers. It's genuinely tough to pull off solo since the mannequins are spread across both sides of the map, so it usually takes a coordinated effort from the whole lobby.

title: The RC-XD Is the Only Low-Level Killstreak That Can Actually Get You a Kill Yourself
description: Most three-kill streaks in Black Ops just give you information, like a Spy Plane. The RC-XD breaks that pattern completely, handing you a remote-controlled car packed with explosives that you drive straight into enemies before blowing it up. It's the only reward at that low a killstreak tier that lets you rack up an actual kill with your own hands rather than just intel.

title: Black Ops Let You Gamble Your Own Currency on Matches
description: Wager Match was one of the odder additions to the original Black Ops multiplayer, letting six players throw their CoD Points into a pot before a match and split the winnings based on where they finished. First place walked away with half the pool, second got thirty percent, and third took the rest, while anyone outside the top three lost their buy-in entirely.

title: One Multiplayer Map Lets You Hack Your Way Into the Enemy Spawn
description: The Skylines map isn't just a static backdrop. Players can interact with the building's security systems to lock or unlock doors, uncover hidden rooms, and even drive an RC-XD through secret corridors that lead straight toward the other team's spawn point, turning a simple killstreak toy into a sneaky infiltration tool.

title: Mob of the Dead Cast Four Prohibition-Era Gangsters Trying to Break Out of Alcatraz
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Rather than reusing any of the established zombies crew, the Mob of the Dead map builds a completely self-contained story around four mobsters locked up on Alcatraz during Prohibition. They're in the middle of executing a daring escape plan the same night a zombie outbreak hits the island, turning their jailbreak into a fight for survival instead.

title: Mob of the Dead's Gangsters Are Voiced by Actual Mob Movie Legends
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Treyarch didn't hold back on casting for Mob of the Dead, bringing in Michael Madsen, Joe Pantoliano, Chazz Palminteri, and Ray Liotta to voice and perform motion capture for the four convicts at the center of the map. It's the kind of lineup you'd expect from an actual gangster film rather than a zombies DLC pack.

title: Mob of the Dead Is the Only Zombies Map You Can Finish Without Dying
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: The main story quest on Mob of the Dead, called Pop Goes the Weasel, is built around the characters' escape attempt, and completing it lets players actually end the game and walk away alive rather than eventually getting overwhelmed by the horde. At the time, it was the first instance in zombies history where survival, not death, was the built-in ending.

title: Mob of the Dead Swaps Quick Revive for Actual Ghost Powers
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Because the usual Quick Revive perk doesn't exist on this map, going down instead triggers Afterlife Mode, letting your character float around as a ghost to flip switches, revive teammates remotely, or scout ahead before returning to your body. It effectively replaces one system with a much more involved one built specifically for the map's prison setting.

title: There's a Melee Weapon Made From a Prison Spoon That Rivals the Best Guns in the Game
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Buried inside Mob of the Dead's side objectives is the Golden Spork, a melee weapon that can one-hit kill zombies all the way up to round 34. For a game mode built around ever-escalating waves of undead, that puts a literal prison utensil just behind the upgraded One Inch Punch from Origins as the strongest melee option zombies has ever had.

title: Black Ops 4 Was the First Mainline Game With No Single-Player Campaign
description: For the first time in the franchise's history, Black Ops 4 shipped without a traditional story campaign at all, putting everything into Multiplayer, Zombies, and a brand new battle royale mode instead. It was a genuinely risky move for a series that had built its reputation on cinematic single-player set pieces.

title: Black Ops 4's Campaign Was Almost a Totally Different Game Called 'Career'
description: Before landing on the battle royale route, Treyarch had actually been building a mode called Career meant to continue Black Ops III's story, set in a post-apocalyptic 2070s and built around 2v2 combat between two rival factions. It got scrapped in early 2018 over technical issues and rough playtest feedback, which is what opened the door for Blackout to take its place.

title: Blackout's Map Is Over a Thousand Times Bigger Than Nuketown
description: Treyarch stitched together locations pulled from across the entire Black Ops series to build Blackout's map, and the result dwarfs anything the franchise had done before. According to the game's own reveal, the battle royale map ended up more than 1,500 times the size of the tiny Nuketown map from the original Black Ops.

title: Black Ops 6's Signature Movement System Can't Be Switched Off
description: Omnimovement lets players sprint, slide, and dive in literally any direction instead of just forward, and it runs across campaign, multiplayer, and zombies alike. Treyarch confirmed there's no toggle for it either, since the studio considers it a core part of how the whole game is built rather than an optional feature players can turn down.

title: A Wheelchair-Bound Frank Woods Mentors the New Hero in Black Ops 6
description: Set in the early 90s, Black Ops 6's campaign brings back Frank Woods as an older, wheelchair-using mentor figure guiding new protagonist Troy Marshall through the story. Russell Adler also returns, tying the game back into the world Cold War had built years earlier while handing the spotlight to a new lead character.

title: Origins Rewrites the Zombies Timeline Around Giant WWI Robots
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: The Origins zombies map ties the entire mythology back to the First World War, where the discovery of Element 115 in northern France lets Group 935 scientists build thousand-foot-tall robots decades before anything similar should exist. It reframes the whole zombies storyline as starting much earlier in history than players had assumed.

title: Origins' Three Giant Robots Are Named After Norse Gods
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: The trio of massive robots stomping around the Origins map aren't just nameless set pieces, they're called Freya, Odin, and Thor, and each one can crush zombies or knock down players unlucky enough to be standing under a descending foot. Getting caught in the wrong spot when one steps down is one of the map's more brutal running hazards.

title: The Game's Creepy 'Numbers Station' Plot Point Is Based on Something Real
description: Mason's mission to decode a mysterious numbers broadcast isn't just a Hollywood invention. Numbers stations are a genuine Cold War phenomenon, shortwave radio channels that read out strings of digits believed to carry coded messages to field agents, and some have never been officially explained even decades later.

title: Cold War's Villain Is Loosely Based on an Unidentified Real Soviet Spy
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: Perseus, the shadowy antagonist hunting nukes across Europe, borrows his name and premise from a real code name the CIA once used for a suspected Soviet spy believed to have infiltrated the Manhattan Project and passed along nuclear secrets. His identity was never confirmed in real life, which left the game plenty of room to build its own fictional version of him.

title: Cold War's First Trailer Used Real Footage of an Actual KGB Defector
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: Rather than opening with in-game cinematics, the earliest teaser for Black Ops Cold War was built around genuine archival interview footage of Yuri Bezmenov, a real KGB informant who defected to the West in 1970. Splicing real Cold War history into a marketing trailer for a game about spies was a bold way to set the tone before a single frame of gameplay showed up.

title: The Broadcast Ship Trying to Trigger America's Sleeper Agents Has Its Own Name
description: The numbers broadcasts driving Project Nova come from a Soviet spy vessel called the Rusalka, anchored in Cuban waters and secretly acting as the surface cover for an underwater submarine base doubling as the real transmission point. Mason's mission to stop the broadcasts culminates in an airstrike against the ship itself.

title: Frank Woods Got a New Voice for Cold War, and His Original Actor Wasn't Happy About It
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War
description: James C. Burns had voiced Frank Woods for over a decade, going all the way back to the original Black Ops, but Activision never reached out to him about reprising the role for Cold War. Burns later said publicly he wished he'd gotten the chance, since nobody else had the years of backstory with the character that he'd built up.

title: The Interrogation Chair Intro Has Barely Changed in Over a Decade
description: The main menu sequence where you're strapped to a chair and have to mash the triggers to break free was carried almost untouched into the 2026 remaster on newer consoles. The button-mashing trick and the terminal codes behind it work exactly the same way they did back in 2010, meaning fifteen-year-old guides for it still apply nearly word for word.

title: Nuketown Zombies Quietly Happens at the Same Time as the Moon Map's Ending
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: The bonus Nuketown Zombies map doesn't sit off on its own timeline. According to its background lore, the events there play out simultaneously with the ending shown on the original Black Ops' Moon loading screen, quietly linking a small bonus map to one of the series' bigger zombies cliffhangers.

title: You Don't Even Get a Fixed Faction on Nuketown Zombies
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Unlike other zombies maps where you play as a named character, Nuketown Zombies just drops you in as an anonymous CIA or CDC operative, and which side you get assigned to is randomized at the start of every match. It keeps the map feeling detached from the rest of the cast, more like a self-contained drill than part of the main story.

title: The Pack-a-Punch Machine on Nuketown Just Falls Out of the Sky
entertainment: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
description: Most zombies maps make you build or unlock the Pack-a-Punch machine through some kind of puzzle. Nuketown skips all of that entirely: an air raid siren sounds partway through the match and the machine crash-lands randomly somewhere on the map, usually in the backyard or garage, forcing players to scramble toward wherever it happens to land.

title: Zombies Started as a Side Project Nobody Expected to Matter
description: Zombies mode wasn't originally built with much confidence behind it. It began at Treyarch during World at War as a bonus mode made by a small group of developers just messing around, and many on the team assumed a zombie survival mode would land poorly in a serious military shooter. It ended up being popular enough that Black Ops expanded it into a much bigger, better-supported feature with multiple launch maps and ongoing DLC.

title: There's a Secret Song Hidden Behind a Row of Barrels on the World War Maps
description: In the Black Ops remasters of the original World at War zombies maps, shooting down all nine red barrels lined up outside the bunker unlocks the hidden track 'Undone.' It's one of several secret songs scattered across those early maps, most of which require some oddly specific action, like flushing a toilet the right number of times, to trigger.

title: The Rushed Tutorial Nobody Wanted
description: The Temple of Trials, the opening dungeon almost everyone complains about, only exists because Interplay's publishers took one look at the finished game and demanded a proper tutorial. The devs had to bang it out in a matter of days right before launch, which is basically why it feels bolted on. It's still one of the most hated openings in RPG history.

title: The Sniper Rifle That Became a Machine Gun
description: The Bozar was supposed to be a slow, accurate sniper rifle. Somewhere during development someone accidentally flagged it for burst fire instead, turning it into this absurd automatic hand-cannon. The team liked the happy accident so much they just left it broken, and it became one of the best late-game weapons in the game.

title: NPCs Named After Real Trivia Contest Winners
description: Before launch, Black Isle ran a Fallout trivia contest online and through an Australian gaming mag. The two winners, Lucas Kawarski from Poland and Cameron Rapmund from Australia, got themselves written into the game as actual villagers in Arroyo. A later patch even swapped the placeholder names Dumar and Standing Fist for Cameron and Lucas to make the tribute official.

title: Gecko in a Can
description: At the Fallout 2 launch party, guests were handed a promotional plush gecko stuffed into a tin can, made to look like a bit of wasteland snack food. The original idea was actually 'dog meat in a can', but the team couldn't source a decent dog plush in time, so the gecko got the job instead.

title: Ethyl Wright's Name Isn't an Accident
description: Ethyl Wright, whose family runs a moonshine still she personally can't stand, is named after ethanol, the actual chemical name for the alcohol her family distills. It's a quiet little pun that a lot of players walk straight past without noticing.

title: A Reputation That Does Absolutely Nothing
description: If you play through the game without sleeping with anyone, you can earn the reputation title 'Virgin of the Wastes.' It sounds like it should matter, but it's purely cosmetic flavour text with zero effect on dialogue, quests, or stats. Pure bragging rights only.

title: A Crashed Star Trek Away Team
description: Wander far enough and you can stumble on a special encounter where a shuttlecraft called the USS Torres has crash-landed, surrounded by three dead crewmen in red uniforms.
